items.title: Verstappen takes first 2026 pole ahead of Hamilton
items.content: <article>Max Verstappen takes his and Red Bull's first pole position of 2026 with an imperious performance in qualifying at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.</article>
items.lbText:
Max Verstappen took his and Red Bull's first pole position of 2026 with an imperious performance in qualifying at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton.

Verstappen, whose last pole and victory was at the season finale in Abu Dhabi in 2026, was 0.298 seconds quicker than Hamilton after topping all three sessions of qualifying.

Red Bull's Isack Hadjar was third fastest but has a five-place grid penalty, which will promote runaway championship leader Kimi Antonelli to third place.

The Italian's closest rival, team-mate George Russell, could manage only eighth fastest.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc was fifth fastest, ahead of the McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.

Fernando Alonso, fresh from confirming he will stay in F1 for at least another year in 2027, gave Aston Martin their best qualifying position of the year with 12th place, behind Alpine's Pierre Gasly, Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto and Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson.

The second Aston Martin of Lance Stroll was 14th, split from Alonso by Williams' Carlos Sainz.

Red Bull introduced a aerodynamic upgrade at the last race in Azerbaijan, and it has proved to be a major step forward at the demanding Sepang track, hosting this race after it was postponed earlier in the year because of the war in the Middle East.

Verstappen has had a difficult year, struggling for pace and balance for much of it, but he is on a strong run of results after steady improvements to the car.

"Fantastic," he said. "We have been trying many grands prix to get pole, sometimes a bit closer than others. But to finally get it from where we started the season, pretty incredible."

Hamilton's position on the front row revives memories of their bitter title battle in 2021, when the seven-time champion was at Mercedes, and whets appetites for the grand prix on Sunday.

Hamilton said: "It's so hot here. That's made it a massive challenge for the cars, the tyres, the mechanics in the garage.

"Because the tyres are sliding, it's so hard to find a good balance and we made one change and we finally hit the sweet spot."

Mercedes have brought their first major upgrade since the Canadian Grand Prix in June, but it has not proved the step forward hoped.

Unusally, Antonelli went into qualifying with only four new sets of soft tyres rather than the usual five and compromised his programme by having his first lap in second session deleted for going beyond track limits.

That meant he had to use another set of tyres in the session, which left him only one for the final shootout.

He went out in the middle of the session, after the others did their first runs, and ended up with a time 0.501secs from pole, much further away than Mercedes would have hoped.

Antonelli said: "It's a shame because with only one set, big pressure. I did what I could but with another set we could have fought for front row. Not P1, because Max was too quick today."

But he fared better than Russell, who was lacking pace compared to his team-mate all day, and ended up 0.240secs off Antonelli.

The Briton said: "It's the most demanding circuit on the tyres, so we don't know exactly why we didn't have the pace. From Friday it was clear we weren't on the pace of the Red Bulls and we haven't really progressed. The others have caught up and overtaken [us]."

It was also a difficult day for McLaren, who were tipped by Russell as the potential frontrunners going into the weekend because of their car's strong recent performances on tracks that share characteristics with this one.

But they lacked pace all weekend and Norris could manage only a best lap of 0.627secs off the pace.

For Aston Martin, though, this was confirmation that changes they have made to their car in recent races have borne fruit.

They struggled in Italy and Azerbaijan because their Honda engine remains the worst in the field, despite two recent upgrades.

But on a track where power sensitivity is lower, the improvements to the chassis made in terms of aerodynamics and weight since the summer added up.

A lap by Alonso that was 1.524secs off the pace is by far their strongest performance of the year, and a suggestion that the veteran's faith they could step forward significantly in 2027 has some foundation.

"It was definitely one the best qualifying of the year," Alonso said. "1.5secs to top of Q2, so smallest margin. It seems this circuit is a little better for our package and let's see tomorrow if we can take advantage of this."

items.title: 'The world caves in on you' - Ion Izagirre reflects on broken wrist injury that wrecked end of 17-year career
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
In any other circumstances for the 37-year-old Basque racer, an accident and injuries suffered on Wednesday when out training would have been a major setback to his plans, but by no means impossible to overcome. But this time round, the broken left wrist that Izagirre ended up with after falling during training has much more serious long-term consequences.

In a flash, and barely ten days before Il Lombardia, his plans for a dream farewell to his days as a roadracer at the last Monument of 2026 have all gone up in smoke. That he was in excellent condition - witness his victory at the Memorial Pantani a month back - only makes it all a tougher pill to swallow. But it's the completely wrong-footed ending to his career that is what is perhaps hardest to handle of all.

"I was out training, doing one of my last rides for the last races of the year," the Cofidis pro told, "and on a downhill that was a bit wet, my back wheel went from underneath me.

"I was trying to stop myself from going down as I fell and that's when I broke my wrist. It doesn't hurt, and I had a splint put on it at the hospital. But that was that."

The injury made it out of the question that he could start the three Italian races he had left on his program as a pro, Coppa Agostini on October 4, Tre Valli Varesine (October 6) and Il Lombardia (October 11) - where he has two top ten places in his career, including a fourth in 2024. As ends of careers go, so close to the finish line, you'd need a heart of stone not to feel that this was a truly harsh twist of fate.

What made it worse, the Cofidis racer told was that he was in great condition "and hoping to do something good to round it all off with a good taste, at least give it 100% and finish my career, too, riding a bike, not like this."

"But that's how it plays out sometimes. You never want it, never expect it, but sometimes that's just what happens."

Il Lombardia clearly is a Classic that suits him, too and after the big boost to his motivation he'd had from winning the Memorial, he was raring to get back into racing one last time.

"The Italian races I'd done before, I was going well, but I wasn't at the level I wanted, maybe because of the heat or whatever. I couldn't show what I'd got," he said.

"But then the weather changed; it turned rainier and cooler, and my body really responded, and in Pantani I was always up there, getting in the moves and so on.

"Then in the last moment, when four of us went ahead, I could play it out well in the sprint. So by then I knew I was on a roll, and it made me feel confident for what was to come."

That could hardly have changed more dramatically after his accident on Wednesday, out training alone and building his form one last time. His morale now, he agrees, is that of feeling screwed.

"Yes, above all yesterday when it all happened. I dunno, I just couldn't believe it. When I couldn't hold the handlebar with my left hand, I realised it was to my season and my career. The world caves in on you.

"I didn't want to finish my career with a plaster on my wrist. I wanted to finish it enjoying my racing in the Italian races. But it's not going to happen that time."

His only way of trying to fight back against the misery is, as he says, that he's received lots of messages of support and sympathy, also reminding him that he's had an exceptionally good last season and to try and focus on that.

They're not wrong, either. Apart from Pantani, Izagirre had both been consistent and taken another top-level one-day race, the GP Miguel Indurain, along with a fourth place overall in the Itzulia Basque Country, a seventh in Flèche Wallonne and a sixth in Eschborn-Frankfurt this season. He also raced the Tour de France - a race where he's twice been a stage winner - taking part in breakaways up until the last day in the Alps.

"But maybe it's a bit too soon to try and feel upbeat," Izagirre said, "instead right now you could say I'm in mourning. It's just a feeling of being hurt and demotivated, disappointed with what happened.

"Maybe further down the line, looking at things more objectively, I'll value this last season, what I've done in it, a lot more."

If road racing is now out of the question - and with it the celebrations and farewell dinner he and the team had planned after Lombardia - he hasn't totally lost hope of perhaps ending the very last chapter of his career as he wanted. That will be a cyclo-cross event held each year on October 25 in his home town of Ormaiztegi in the Basque Country. "There are still 25 days and let's hope that's possible that I recover in time," he said, "maybe that way I'd finish it all off at home."

"I've been able to race it in the last few years, which is something that wasn't possible before then because the teams were more worried about the risks of crashes and injuries and so on.

"But when I've been able to do it, I've done it, and this year even more so, as it's my last chance. Let's see if I'll be able to do it again, for one last time."

After that, what is out of the question, he said, is turning to an alternative career in gravel or cyclo-cross in the future. His only 'career plan' right now is to be with his family and then, he reckons, other ideas will come up. But in terms of racing, as he said, "When I hang up my wheels, that's me done for good. I'll go on riding a bike out of pure pleasure, and as a fan of the sport."

"Cycling has given me a lot, and I think it'll help me clear my head if I need it in the future, too, by simply riding the bike. But without any need of being out there doing series, training hard and so on. Just choosing the day and the place and the time and the people I want to be with. It'll be another world."

items.title: Alex Marquez gets hefty penalty for multi-bike Motegi crash
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Gresini Ducati rider Alex Marquez will serve a double long-lap penalty in Sunday's Japanese Grand Prix at Motegi for causing a multi-bike crash in the sprint.

Marquez was attacking fellow Ducati rider Fabio Di Giannantonio for sixth place coming into Turn 3 on the opening lap, but ran out of room to navigate the corner as Pedro Acosta cut back in after being forced to the outside by Bastianini.

Marquez thus lost the front in trying desperately to slow down, hitting Acosta, before his bike then also collected Di Giannantonio on the outside.

He will retain fifth on the grid on Sunday but will be compromised by a double long-lap assessed by the Simon Crafar-led stewards' panel, despite this being a first offence this season for the Gresini man.

Incidentally, the crash eliminated Marquez's future KTM team-mate in Di Giannantonio and his future employer's lead rider in Acosta.

Other double long-lap penalties this season included one for Joan Mir for ignoring a black-and-orange flag and ones for Jorge Martin and Johann Zarco for causing multi-rider pile-ups at the start.

Speaking to media after the sprint, Acosta said that incidents like these happened in racing but semi-chastised Marquez for "trying to get a podium quite early".

He also lamented a lost opportunity to make up points on third-placed-in-the-standings Marco Bezzecchi, believing that a podium - though likely not a win - was on the cards had he stayed on.

Marquez, meanwhile, said he accepted the penalty and that he had made a mistake, and apologised for ending his rivals' races.

items.title: Nil Gimeno snares first professional win at stage 7 of Le Tour de Langkawi to Batu Pahat
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
Nil Gimeno (Equipo Kern Pharma) took his first professional victory on stage 7 of Le Tour de Langkawi to Batu Pahat, as the break of four prevailed despite a charged pursuit by the sprinters teams.

Gimeno, who was a frustrating fourth on stage 4 when the break survived in the Cameron Highlands, wasn't going to let a second opportunity slip him by. This time he got to celebrate rather than commiserate as he crossed the line ahead of Mario Aparicio (Burgos Burpellet-BH) in second and Andrei Stepanov (Wheeltop Rotor Chengdu) in third. The remaining member of the break, Adne van Engelen (Terengganu), was the one who this time had to settle for fourth.

"We came here for a stage victory," an elated Gimeno, who couldn't get the smile off his face, told reporters after the stage. "I thought it was the best opportunity the fourth day, but it came today, so I'm over the moon."

The quartet upset the sprinters plans after going out early as part of a group of seven and it was a hard-earned second break win of the tour. None of the four took the foot off the accelerator pedal until the race was done and Gimeno had claimed the first Spanish stage win of the race, which is in its 30th edition, with an impressive turn of speed.

"I know I'm really fast, but you never know when you go full gas all the day," said Gimeno. "You don't know if you have the strength in the sprint but luckily, all the riders in the breakaway, we committed ... each one of them went full gas all the way."

The final day of racing in stage 8 on Sunday is expected to deliver a sprint showdown, although there is a category 3 climb at 50km to go that once again has some potential to create a tempting launch point for those looking for one last roll of the dice at the Malaysian ProTour race.

Lennart Jasch (Tudor Pro Cycling) enters the deciding stage with his grip on the leader's jersey remaining firm as he kept his 26 second gap to Alex Balderstone (Caja Rural-Seguros RGA) intact on stage 7. Jasch claimed the jersey on stage 2, and hasn't put a foot wrong since, but is not prepared to start celebrating a potential GC victory, on his first attempt as leader, just yet.

"I don't really dare to speak too much about it because today on paper it was an easy day but it was a really hard day so in the end its a bike race like every other day and tomorrow, for sure it won't be easy," said Jasch at the post stage media conference. "There are still a lot of things that can happen."

There were 109 riders starting the stage in the historic but vibrant location of Melaka, and sadly one of the missing riders, Ronan Auge (Unibet Rose Rockets) was in hospital after crashing on stage 6, with his squad saying that while his condition is currently stable and not life-threatening he was being "kept in a medically induced coma to optimise his treatment".

After the racing started, Aiman Rosli (Terengganu) was the first rider off the mark, determined to get into the break particularly with the first intermediate sprint at his home town, Tangkak, at 45km into the day of racing. Plenty of others, however, had the same idea.

There were twists and turns when it came to forming a lead group but by the time the race was 28km in a break of seven had formed which included Mario Aparicio (Burgos Burpellet-BH), Nil Gimeno (Kern Pharma), Santiago Herreño (Bardiani CSF 7 Saber) Adne van Engelen and Kee Zhe Yie of Terengganu, Andrei Stepanov (Wheeltop Rotor Chengdu) and George Matsui (Aisan).

Matsui and Kee fell away, making it a group of five with 2:25 to the peloton at 30km to go and then Herreño was next.

It was a determined chase from behind but they were only making gradual inroads. No matter what torture the XDS-Astana team and Modern Adventure squad were putting themselves through so Matteo Malucelli and Riley Pickrell could face-off in another sprint, it didn't seem to be enough.

They still had more than a kilometre at 35 seconds to go after working together flawlessly to make sure the break survived for a second time at the 2026 edition of Le Tour de Langkawi.

*Cyclingnews attended Le Tour de Langkawi on an invitation/media package from the race that included travel and accommodation. In line with our editorial standards, our coverage is independent and was not subject to review, approval or influence by the organiser or any sponsor; no favourable coverage was promised or given in return.

items.title: Thrown in with Giggs and Beckham: how Manchester United tried to get Billy Kenny
items.author: Billy Kenny
items.content:
Former Everton midfielder, known as the ‘Goodison Gazza’, recalls being made to feel special by Alex Ferguson in this autobiography extract

“So this is the scouser ya been goin’ on aboot then …” My face turned Manchester United red. Scanning the room full of smiles and staring eyes, I identified the mystery Scottish voice as the man who’d just become the first player to score more than 20 league goals for the club since George Best in the 1960s. “Good answer,” replied Brian McClair after following up on my smile and nod by asking whether I supported Everton or Liverpool. “Ye’ll dee well ’ere laddie.”

Brian Kidd had just introduced me to the Man United first team by silencing the room to draw attention to my presence. “Lads, this is Billy from up the road,” he said. I was still starstruck from seeing all these famous faces as my chauffeur for the day, Eric Harrison, pulled up in the car park at The Cliff a few minutes earlier. Paul McGrath. Mark Hughes. Bryan Robson. Kevin Moran. Norman Whiteside. I ticked them all off in my head. Thank fuck I was developing an ear for everyday Glaswegian because after a bit of piss-taking from the first-teamers about being a scouser, I found myself standing in an office at the end of a short and narrow corridor, shaking hands with another one.

items.title: Marquez beats penalised Martin in Motegi sprint, Moreira stars
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Ducati MotoGP rider Marc Marquez took five points out of a penalised Jorge Martin's championship lead with a commanding win in the Motegi sprint.

Marquez picked off Martin at the start, setting up the move through Turn 1 and completing it through Turn 2.

No real victory battle materialised from there as Marquez established a one-second buffer and managed it from there on out, with Martin looking to settle what should have been - but wasn't - an equally-comfortable second place.

Both anyway gained significant ground on outside title hopeful Marco Bezzecchi, who had a very poor race despite being aided by attrition.

Three rivals were removed from the podium battle as, after being overtaken into Turn 3 by Enea Bastianini, Pedro Acosta cut back in to take the corner and was then wiped out by a too-fast Alex Marquez, with Fabio Di Giannantonio also taken down.

But Bezzecchi was one of two riders to have selected the medium rear for the race in lieu of the soft, and the choice proved downright disastrous.Third after the start, he had no pace to stay with the leading duo and was swallowed up by Bastianini, as well as Diogo Moreira and Ai Ogura.

Moreira had overtaken Ogura while the latter was trying to make his way past Bezzecchi, and then set off after a podium. He reeled in Bastianini towards the end, and both suddenly closed in massively on Martin.

Neither made the move, but both Martin and Bastianini fell foul of track limits on the final lap, catching the green paint coming off the kerb at Turn 10 - and thus promoting Moreira to a remarkable second place.

The penalties meant Martin is now only seven points ahead of Marquez, with Bezzecchi 45 down on his team-mate.

Ogura took fifth place ahead of Bezzecchi, followed by Johann Zarco and Raul Fernandez - who had engaged in a back-and-forth duel through the race.

Fabio Quartararo snuck into ninth, fending off Fermin Aldeguer late on and ensuring that all five manufacturers scored in the sprint.

The only rider to retire besides the three involved in the opening-lap crash was Pecco Bagnaia, last year's grand prix-and-sprint winner, who ran 13th but came in on the final lap with a shredded rear tyre.

items.title: What went on in final Sepang F1 practice
items.author: Ben Anderson
items.content:
Formula 1 championship leader Kimi Antonelli set the pace in final practice for F1’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, as Mercedes recovered from its most difficult Friday of 2026 to lead the way with its heavily upgraded car.

Deputy team principal Bradley Lord said Mercedes conducted overnight simulator work to figure out why the upgrades had improved medium- and high-speed corner performance but at the expense of the low-speed turns, which he described as a previous strength of the car.

And it would seem that work was successful, as Antonelli became the first driver to lap below 1m37 seconds so far this weekend. On his second set of soft tyres he set a 1m36.302s best to end the session fastest.

Red Bull continued its strong practice form in FP3, with Max Verstappen second-fastest but almost three tenths down on Antonelli.

Verstappen’s team-mate Isack Hadjar backed that up with the third-fastest time. He complained of the recently upgraded RB22 being “so unpredictable” through Turns 1 and 9 early on, before ending the session 0.558s off the pace.

George Russell was only fourth in the other Mercedes, six tenths off Antonelli, while the Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton rounded out the top six, seven tenths off the pace and separated by just 0.025s.

With track temperatures running in the mid-50s°C, the tyres were only good for a single flying lap and couldn’t produce better laptimes even after several cool-down laps or time in the pits.

McLaren struggled to extract performance from the soft compound in FP3 and ended up seventh and eighth, with Lando Norris setting his best lap on the medium (C3) tyre. He was eight tenths off the pace, while team-mate Oscar Piastri was a full second off Antonelli, having only found a tenth of a second going from medium to soft.

After a Friday spent solely focused on high-fuel long runs owing to a hefty grid penalty he faces for this race, Franco Colapinto led the way in the midfield for Alpine, 1.6s off the pace, ahead of Arvid Lindblad’s Racing Bulls and the Audi of Gabriel Bortoleto.

And Fernando Alonso indicated Aston Martin might be a Q2 threat at Sepang by setting the 12th-fastest time FP3, just over three tenths down on Colapinto’s Alpine and 0.018s up on Pierre Gasly’s.

items.title: MotoGP Japanese GP: Martin edges out Marquez to claim back-to-back pole positions
Martin upsets Marquez to score surprise Motegi pole
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
MotoGP championship leader Jorge Martin sniped Motegi pole position from title rival Marc Marquez after a substantial turnaround from Friday practice.

Martin, who was only eighth-fastest on Friday, maximised the final sector on his second Q2 run to jump ahead of Marquez by a tenth, securing the new Motegi pole record in the process.

Marquez had held provisional Japanese Grand Prix pole after the opening runs, but couldn't improve on his second Q2 outing - which included a trip into the gravel at Turn 3.

Third title contender Marco Bezzecchi took a front-row spot for the briefest of moments in the end, before surrendering it right away to Pedro Acosta, who had used Bezzecchi as reference.

Alex Marquez (Gresini Ducati) completed a top five covered by just 0.175s, ahead of Fabio Di Giannantonio (VR46 Ducati), Enea Bastianini (Tech3 KTM), and Q1 graduate Raul Fernandez (Trackhouse Aprilia).

LCR team-mates Diogo Moreira and Johann Zarco were next up, Zarco crashing in Q2, while Ai Ogura - who, like team-mate Fernandez, advanced from Q1 - and Fabio Quartararo rounded out the Q2 order.

Yellow flags triggered by a fast Brad Binder crash entering the Turns 12-13-14 sequence nearly compromised Fernandez in Q1 and nearly put defending Motegi winner Pecco Bagnaia through into Q2 instead - but Fernandez had enough time to go again and consign Bagnaia to fifth row on the grid.

Joining him on that row will be Ducati stablemate Franco Morbidelli and Q1 standout Somkiat Chantra. Chantra, riding as Joan Mir's substitute rider at the factory Honda team, produced a better qualifying result than any of his efforts in his full-time season in 2025 - and outqualified team-mate Luca Marini in the process.

It was a disappointing run to 18th on the grid for Fermin Aldeguer, as he outqualified only the returning Maverick Vinales and three Yamahas.

items.title: USA gets another UCI race as Battenkill returns to pro calendar
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
One year after returning to the domestic pro calendar, the Battenkill road race in New York State is back on the UCI calendar after a 13-year absence, giving another boost for professional cycling in North America.

The race will run on May 22, 2027, as a UCI 1.2-ranked men's race, two weeks before the Armed Forces Cycling Classic Capitol Cup, also a men's 1.2 race, will be held on June 5.

The return of Battenkill follows the revival of the Philadelphia Cycling Classic p/b Amerigas, UCI 1.1-ranked road races for men and women. Together with the Tour of the Gila men's and women's 2.2-ranked stage races, these are the only US events currently listed on the UCI's 2027 road calendar.

As of yet, the Gran Premio New York City is not listed on the UCI's calendar, but organisers assured Cyclingnews that the application was submitted for a 1.2-ranked men's event, scheduled for May 16, 2027.

Battenkill, formerly known as Tour of the Battenkill, was held as a UCI race twice before, the first time in 2010, when Caleb Fairly soloed to the win ahead of Floyd Landis. Francisco Mancebo won the other edition in 2012. The event continued as a gran fondo in intervening years under different ownership, but the 2027 edition brings it back into the hands of Anthem Sports.

"Bringing Battenkill back to the UCI calendar has been one of our major goals since returning the event to Cambridge," event director Dieter Drake said. "Battenkill was built around hard, unpredictable racing on beautiful but unforgiving roads. The UCI race gives us an opportunity to bring that experience back to professional riders while also introducing a new generation of cyclists to what makes this event so special."

Organisers compare the course to the Belgian classics, where numerous short, steep climbs, narrow roads and unpaved sections favour positioning, tactics and the ability to endure repeated efforts.

"There isn't one climb where you can say the race will be decided," Drake said. "The entire course makes the selection. Riders are constantly being asked to make decisions - where to position themselves, when to spend energy, how aggressively to ride the dirt and when to attack. That has always been the essence of Battenkill."

The 2027 race will be based around the village of Cambridge, with a full weekend of events for amateur racers and recreational riders, and Drake hopes it will become a long-term fixture on the calendar.

"We aren't trying to reinvent Battenkill," Drake said. "We're trying to preserve what made people remember it. Cambridge, the dirt roads, the farms, the weather, the climbs and the unpredictability are all part of the race. Bringing the UCI event back gives us the opportunity to build on that history rather than replace it."

items.title: Evans names Solberg the “danger man” in WRC title fight
Lachlan Morton set to leave EF Education-EasyPost
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
Lachlan Morton, one of the most popular riders of the EF Education-EasyPost squad, revealed that he is leaving the team after six seasons with the US outfit. The ultra-endurance specialist told that his victory in the 3-Peaks endurance cyclocross race in Yorkshire last weekend was his "last time pinning on a number with EF".

Morton began his career as part of the organisation when it was Garmin-Sharp after racing for the development squad, but turned his focus to pushing his body in long-distance challenges beginning in 2014. He returned to the WorldTour in 2017 and then returned to EF Education in 2019.

But the lonely road didn't stop calling, and in 2021 Morton completed the entire Tour de France route - including transfers - solo. It marked the start of a different relationship with the team, completing various long-distance challenges and gravel races instead of racing in the WorldTour.

With his time in pink ending, the 34-year-old will continue to perform superhuman feats of endurance around the globe, telling that he has an eye on Pakistan, Papua New Guinea and Ecuador for his future adventures.

First, Morton will attempt to follow the Pony Express route - a 3,164-kilometre ride from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Sacramento, California, beginning on Monday, October 5, the EF Education-EasyPost team announced on Friday. The route was used in the 1860s by young riders on horseback who carried mail across Missouri, Kansas, Nebraska, Colorado, Wyoming, Nevada and into California.

"You start on the plains, essentially, coming across Kansas, then across the basin through Wyoming, into Utah," Morton said in the team's press release. "The real crux is the Nevada section - the stretch from Salt Lake City across to Carson City - because it's incredibly remote and very exposed. There's a lot that could go wrong there, and you're very much on your own. That's probably the hardest part.

"Then you cross the Sierra Nevada on the southern side of Lake Tahoe and drop through the foothills, which I know well because I live out there now, and finish in Sacramento."

The fastest time on horseback was set in 1861 at seven days, 17 hours, but the route fell out of use after the first telegraph lines were completed and eliminated the need for rapid hand-delivered messages.

"The way they could get mail across the country at that speed - before there was any railroad connecting it – was revolutionary," Morton said.

"The idea of people traversing such massive distances just captured my imagination, especially knowing a lot of that terrain. Think of these big open spaces - huge plains, mountain ranges - and you imagine a slow transition, but with the elevation and the vegetation it's always evolving, and when you're covering big distances you get a really diverse variety of riding. It's a great canvas for adventure. It's existed there for so long, and you feel like you're participating in what the country is all about."

Morton is familiar with at least some of the route, having set the fastest time on the Tour Divide from Alberta to New Mexico in 2023, although his time has since been eclipsed.

In his Pony Express attempt, Morton will deliver letters along the route just to fully embrace the origins of the route.

"The appeal for me is the history of it," Morton said. "It's wild to get into that mindset – you're a kid trying to make some money, and there's this opportunity to ride a horse with a mochila full of mail through the night for 75 miles (120 kilometres) flat out, across remote, gnarly terrain that no one else has been crossing. It's quite a courageous thing. It's hard to imagine, and that's why I want to go out there and try to get a better understanding of what that would have been like, and the difficulties they faced doing it over 150 years ago."

Just as the riders of old swapped horses to continue at speed, Morton will switch between the Cannondale TopStone gravel bike, his SuperSix lightweight road bike and the Scalpel full-suspension mountain bike.

"The route I've put together tries to get as close to the original as I could. I'm excited because it'll use all the different disciplines I've raced," Morton said.

items.title: The Rapha Meltdown, Worlds Drama, and Selling $6,500 Wheels in 2026 | The Velo Podcast
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Inside the Rapha corporate fallout, Worlds drama, and balancing parenting with training. Plus: The appeal of a custom Firefly rim-brake bike, and how $6,500 Partington wheels can still compete against cheaper Chinese rivals.
items.lbText:
The Velo Podcast wouldn’t happen without subscribers. We’re offering listeners of the show a special 25% discount on an Outside+ membership. Enter the code velopod at checkout to score these savings, and thank you for your support!

You requested road bike content, so this week you’ve got it. Last weekend was Worlds and the race for the rainbow stripes. Logan Jones-Wilkins was in attendance, and Mike Levy, Lisa Charlebois, and I handed him the mic for a breakdown of what he saw. We talk about Brandon McNulty and whether his World Championship win was out of left field or expected. We also discuss Kate Courtney and a ridiculous positional rule that could have completely upended the women’s race.

Before that, we start with some listener questions. We received lots of corrections on the Canyon mounting system, but I argue that the technicalities are irrelevant to the greater point. The Q&A gives me a chance to put on my family-man hat and share advice for riders trying to balance their mileage with time for their kids, while Logan answers for his Haro bike.

Later in the episode, we dive into a couple of topics close to my heart. We start by discussing why the Rapha financial meltdown is a textbook example of a marketing fail, while Logan presents a strong argument for why the recent CEO departure might have actually been a voluntary exit after all. From there, we pivot to high-dollar bling. The new titanium Firefly rim brake bike makes no logical sense in 2026 but still commands attention, while the $5,500 Partington wheels serve as a positive case study on how Western brands can maintain appeal against cheaper Eastern competition.

items.title: Lachlan Morton’s Latest Challenge: Beat the Horses of the Old Pony Express
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: The Australian who calls California home will try to do the 1,900-mile mixed terrain route in just under eight days with a combination of three different types of bikes.
items.lbText:
Morton during his 'Alt Tour' last summer. (Photo: James Startt/VeloNews)

Lachlan Morton , in his undying quest to check off an extraordinary ultra-cycling side quest every year, has announced his newest challenge.

Morton will set out to retrace the Pony Express, a foundational route of America’s westward expansion, on October 5.

The Pony Express was the historic route used to deliver mail from the eastern metropolises to the early settlements and cities on the western frontier. Like the horseback riders who relayed mail across the plains, mountains, and forests of the 1,966-mile trek from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Sacramento, California, Morton will travel light and fast.

Additionally, as those riders changed horses every 10 miles of riding, Morton will swap between his road, gravel, and mountain bike on a varied route that is built to resemble the historic route as closely as possible.

To raise the stakes, Morton will be racing the fastest recorded time set by mail carriers back when the Pony Express was in use in the mid 1800s.

“The way they could get mail across the country at that speed—before there was any railroad connecting it—was revolutionary,” Morton said in a press release. “The idea of people traversing such massive distances just captured my imagination, especially knowing a lot of that terrain.

“Think of these big open spaces—huge plains, mountain ranges—and you imagine a slow transition, but with the elevation and the vegetation it’s always evolving, and when you’re covering big distances you get a really diverse variety of riding. It’s a great canvas for adventure.

“It’s existed there for so long, and you feel like you’re participating in what the country is all about.”

The route will start in Missouri, take on the Great Plains of Kansas and Nebraska, before heading into the heart of the Rockies across Wyoming and Utah.

Perhaps the key of the journey, however, will be the long trek across Nevada—one of the most remote areas in the Lower 48—before Morton will finish through the Sierra Nevada, routes he knows well as he now lives in the foothills of California’s Gold Country.

While the route itself is not tied to any particular FKT or event, as his effort at the Tour Divide and Alt Tour were built from, his Pony Express effort will still have a time goal. Morton will be looking to beat the time set by the fastest Pony Express horseback relay.

In 1861, a team of riders and horses made the run from Missouri to California in just seven days and 17 hours to deliver Abraham Lincoln’s inaugural address to California to convince the state to remain a part of the Union as the Civil War loomed. That will be the mark Morton will hope to beat.

The Pony Express was replaced later in 1861 by the first national transcontinental telegraph line, but the mythos of the horseback mailmen lived on as iconography of the Old West. In his effort to take on the same route, Morton is hoping to understand more about what the true experience of the Old West was through the lens of his own riding.

“The appeal for me is the history of it,” he said. “It’s wild to get into that mindset—you’re a kid trying to make some money, and there’s this opportunity to ride a horse with a mochila full of mail through the night for 75 miles flat out, across remote, gnarly terrain that no one else has been crossing.

“It’s quite a courageous thing. It’s hard to imagine, and that’s why I want to go out there and try to get a better understanding of what that would have been like, and the difficulties they faced doing it over 150 years ago.”

Morton will be supported by his brother, filmmaker Gus Morton, who will be documenting the journey for a film and transporting the bikes that Lachlan won’t be riding over any given stretch.

Gus’ support will be limited, but with the remote nature of most of the course, when Lachlan swaps bikes, he will also restock supplies, just as the riders did on the old Pony Express a century and a half ago.

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘Either joint replacement, let it go, or, I guess, amputation’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
My brain melted yesterday, thought it was Sunday, not Thursday.

Anyway, today’s Friday. I guess.

Here’s the latest from Tarrytown as we keep hearing from different Knicks.

On Josh Hart’s injured finger and the toughness it reflects:

“Josh, he’s a handsome young man. But that finger is ugly. So, I don’t look at it. But it adds to his toughness. Josh is a tough son of a gun, man. I can’t even watch when he [shakes his hand], because I’m just like, oh, my gosh I can’t imagine having a finger like that.

“But it just shows who he is. He’s tough but, more importantly, there’s dedication there to wanting to be a great shooter, and you’ve got to put it into work. And he puts in the work, even though his finger’s bothering him. And even though it’s a little crooked, he’s putting in the work to get it right. [Shooting coach] Pete [Patton] and the rest of the coaches are helping him out, and it shows that he can shoot at a high level with the dedication he has in the first place.”

On OG Anunoby’s playoff performance boosting his All-Star case:

“It should help him a ton because guys that are quiet naturally, they have a hard time getting the necessary publicity and promotion toward being an All-Star, unless you’re doing something extraordinary and people start talking about it — like OG in the playoffs. So doing it in the playoffs and having people talk about it should have carryover, in my opinion, since he helped us win the championship.

“And he was in the conversation for [NBA] Finals MVP. That should definitely help create calls for him to have a case to be an All-Star this year. He’s still got to go earn it, but he should be in everybody’s conversation from the beginning.”

On Anunoby’s shooting ability:

“He’s not [at Stephen Curry] or [Klay Thompson’s] level but the next tier. He’s way better than I thought.”

On Anunoby’s confidence, shooting and the Knicks’ spacing:

“His confidence is really high. And I thought during the playoffs we did a really good job of touching the paint and taking the right 3s. With OG being 6-foot-7 with long arms, if you’re closing to him with a smaller guy or a guard, it’s going to be good for us because they try to put their best player on Jalen, and sometimes, their best player is a bigger perimeter defender.

“So that means OG may have a smaller guy [defending him]. That’s not impacting him when he shoots the basketball.

“So I think first starts off with him, yes; he’s way better than what I thought. I would categorize him as a great shooter. But more importantly, I thought our spacing and our ability to touch the paint and spray it helped out a lot.”

On his plans for the preseason games:

“We’ll try to ease them in. The last game is always a dress rehearsal, but we’ll try to build them up leading to that game.”

On the Knicks’ conditioning entering camp after a short summer:

“All the guys look like they’re in pretty good shape, especially for a short summer. We have a conditioning test that we did last year and this year that the guys have to pass to get into camp and they all passed it.”

On James Wiseman’s presence at training camp:

“Fantastic human being, fantastic young man…. Good to see him in the gym. When you’re that long and that athletic, with skill – he has skill – there’s a place for you in this league. Sometimes it takes the right moment, the right team, the right situation, all that stuff, to be able to fit someplace and grow. We have a lot of great guys in camp that have potential of impacting us in a lot of different ways throughout the course of the year. He’s definitely one of the many guys that we have that we’re excited about.”

On Tony Bradley after his training camp signing:

“We’re looking for bigs. Tony’s a veteran guy that’s still in his prime and has a good feel for the game, knows how to play the game the right way and he’s hurt us in the past. To be honest, when a guy hurts you in the past, you tend to remember him more than others. So to be able to add him to camp was a positive for us because again, I said this last year, (Karl-Anthony Towns) has one of the most (challenging positions) out of everybody because I want to move him around when I play him at center. I want to play him at power forward; (when he’s at) power forward 1-4 is interchangeable. Same with OG (Anunoby). OG we put him at the 5 last year. We probably will do it a little bit more this year as well.

“But to be able to do that, you’ve gotta have enough centers around on the team, so having Tony here with his skill set and feel is definitely a blessing because we’re looking at that position heavily.”

On the options to fix his finger:

“The only option for my finger at this point, because of how damaged it is, is a full joint replacement. With a joint replacement, you can’t have the banging, grabbing a rebound, palming it, shooting, catching the ball, doing all that. You can’t do that. So if I did a joint replacement, then I wouldn’t be able to play. So I guess it’s either wrap it until I retire or cut it off. I guess that’s the other option. That’s really the only alternative: either joint replacement, let it go, or, I guess, amputation.

“I mean, there was a lot of stuff that I had to get checked, and that was one of them. It was just with how it deteriorated, the joint and the bone and everything, that’s what it’ll be. So I’ll do that probably when I retire. Hopefully, they can make it straight. You know, it’s a little off center if y’all didn’t realize. So I’m hoping after that joint replacement it can kind of get a little straighter.”

On how the pain in his finger varies from day to day:

“Some days, it’ll be good. Some days it’ll hurt to catch the ball. It varies. I wish I could tell you when I wake up what’s gonna be good, what’s gonna be bad. Somedays it’s good, like a regular functioning finger. And other days it hurts to just close my hand, to make a fist.”

On why a joint replacement would prevent him from playing basketball:

“You can’t have the banging, you know, repetitive, grabbing a rebound, palming it, shooting, catching the ball, doing all that; you can’t do that. It was just with how it deteriorated — the joint and the bone and everything — that’s what it’ll be. So I’ll do that probably when I retire. Hopefully they can make it straight. You know, it’s a little off center if you know y’all didn’t realize.”

On the appearance and functionality of his injured finger:

“I mean, it’s it’s not the prettiest to look at. I would love to have a straight finger, but you know, it works.”

On the physical toll of an NBA career and what fans don’t get:

“I think people think money is everything, and for me, obviously, you want to be compensated fairly for your performance and all that. But at the end of the day, just because you get paid, be blessed in a position to get paid well and take care of our families, [it’s not like] we’re not humans at the same time. I’m sitting here thinking, my knees are aching a little bit, but I want to leave the game and be able to run around and play with my kids when they’re you know 10, 11,12-plus. So that wear and tear, it’s significant to a certain point. If you’re in this league for 14, 15, 16 years, and you see some of these guys that are older, they they got limps, knees are barking, those kind of things. So I think that definitely gets overlooked. But that’s also why I don’t think I’ll play till I’m 40.”

On OG Anunoby’s increased recognition helping his All-Star chances:

“It’s extremely impactful. Obviously, you have to be a gifted and good player to make an All-Star team, but also you have to have the press and all that kind of behind you, bolstering it. So it’s good for people to see how talented he is, how impactful he is on both sides of the ball in the game. So hopefully that recognition will continue throughout this year, and hopefully we’ll be able to get him in.”

On Jalen Brunson’s increased fame following the Knicks title:

“He’s not LeBron, let’s relax.”

On planning to attend Yankees Game 3:

“I think I’m going to be able to get to Game 3. We have a preseason game the next day. So I’m excited, man. I’m excited for New York. Excited for that team.”

On OG Anunoby’s playoff success boosting his confidence:

“That’s definitely a boost of confidence going into this year. OG knows how good he is, and we know how good he is. So he’s gonna continue doing what he does.”

On learning the backcourt rule during his late Game 4 possession:

“I learned on the fly. When I watched the video after, they said you can leave the ball in the backcourt but your body can be in the frontcourt – I didn’t know it was a thing until then. I’m glad it worked out.”

On what has allowed the Knicks to embrace their roles:

“We care for each other, we compete, we want to get each other better”

On whether he always planned to return to the Knicks before signing his extension:

“In my mind, yeah. ‘I want to stay here, I want to stay home.’ We had a chance to do that, and we did it.”

On his championship summer:

“My favorite summer of all time”

items.title: UEC European Championships: Héctor Alvárez solos to victory in under-23 men's road race
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Héctor Álvarez (Spain) produced a powerful, gutsy ride to claim the under-23 European Championships title in Slovenia, attacking away solo in the final 13km to go one better than his result from the World Championships last week.

It wasn't all plain sailing for the 19-year-old, though, as he had originally gone solo with 34.7km to go on Friday, only to be caught on the final time up the tough Možjanca climb, which was tackled three times en route to the finish in Šenčur on Friday.

With Max Bock (Germany) chasing him down on the climb, taking Jan Michal Jackowiak (Poland) and Niels Driesen (Poland) for the ride in his wheel, Álvarez got back in the lead after following an opportunistic move from the Pole, and then countering him with some daring moves into the downhill run off of the climb.

By the time they reached the finish, Álvarez, whose heaps of talent have already seen him confirmed for a step-up to Lidl-Trek's WorldTour squad in 2027, was able to celebrate into the final kilometre as he arrived alone, 20 seconds ahead of Jackowiak.

Driesen left Bock behind in the final 4km to take the bronze medal, adding to his fifth-place finish from Worlds, and earning the Belgians something out of the day after they had done much of the chasing.

"We need to say finally. I was following this for a real long time; it's two years without the win. I think everyone trusted me and I think today I paid it off," said Álvarez, who finished third in the same race a year ago, and was the runner-up in the European junior race two years ago.

"We knew it from the start was going to be crazy and fast, all the flat part, but I think all my team for the first part: óscar, Emilio, Eñaut, Javi, everyone was all there for me; they trusted me from the start, also the team manager. We knew today was the day, and I paid it off.

"I think I don't need to give any advice to the bit guys, but I think you need to be brave. Today I put my way to race that is aggressive, and I finally arrived, so just be brave."

After an aggressive start to the under-23 road race at the UEC European Championships in Slovenia, with several attacks and some crashes at the front of the race, a large group of 60 riders found themselves set to play out three laps of the Šenčur finishing circuit and Možjanca climb (2.1km at 10.2%).

The major selection came on the penultimate time up the climb, which Roberto Capello (Italy) led solo onto, before being bridged across to and dropped by Max Bock (Germany), who rides for Red Bull-Bora-hansgrohe's development team.

Both of them were mopped up by the bubbling chasing pack of favourites past the top of the climb, before everyone felt the brunt of a big counterattack from Spain's Héctor Álvarez with 34.7km to go, carrying his form over from the World Championships in Montreal, where he was second in the same event behind the USA's Ashlin Barry.

Álvarez showed off his strength against the clock as he pushed on solo ahead of the chasing group of 16, who crossed what would be the finish line with a 41-second deficit to make up in the final 22km lap.

Belgium worked in the group behind with four riders remaining, and the gap finally started to go in the right direction for the chasers onto the climb, with Bock working to close the gap down to under 20 seconds with 15km to go. Jan Michal Jackowiak (Poland) and Niels Driesen (Belgium) were the only riders able to follow the German.

Álvarez was caught with 14km to go by the three chasers, but he'd made it over the hardest part of the course on the climb. Despite his grimaces and obvious struggles, the Spaniard kicked straight away again on the plateau, only to be caught by Bock in quick time.

Jackowiak was the next to attack with 13.5km to go into the downhill roads through the trees, with Bock unable to snap onto his wheel as he did to Álvarez. In fact, it was the Spanish rider who still had enough juice to make the junction.

The two bigger men threw some more haymakers at each other on the picturesque downhill run back towards Šenčur, with Álvarez getting separation once again into the last 13km. This ended up being the winning move, with Jackowiak finishing 20 seconds down and Driesen arriving 32 seconds in arrears after a tough race.

items.title: UAE Team Emirates-XRG bolster Classics squad with young Frenchman from Decathlon CMA CGM
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Gautherat turned professional with the French team as a 19-year-old in 2023 and, after winning a stage of the 4 Jours de Dunkerque last year, claimed his first one-day win this year at Paris-Camembert.

More recently, he sprinted to two podiums at the Tour of Luxembourg, the first running Mathieu van der Poel close on a draggy finish.

UAE Team Emirates-XRG are convinced of his potential for the future and have signed him on a three-year contract running through 2029.

"I’m very proud to be joining UAE Team Emirates-XRG. It’s a huge opportunity for me and an exciting new chapter in my career," Gautherat said in a team press release.

"I feel that this is the right environment for me to take another step forward, continue developing as a rider and challenge myself at the highest level. I’m especially motivated by the Classics and I want to keep progressing towards the biggest races and integrate into the squad.

"I’m really looking forward to joining the team, learning from the riders and staff around me and giving everything I can to contribute to the team’s success."

UAE Team Emirates-XRG describe Gautherat as "a powerful rider well suited to the demands of the northern Classics and tough one-day racing."

He got his first taste of the major Classics in his very first season at the age of 20 and the following year he was 11th in both Omloop Het Nieuwsblad and Dwars door Vlaanderen. He has also finished runner-up at the Tro Bro Léon and Classique Dunkerque.

He "will add further depth to UAE Team Emirates-XRG’s Classics group while continuing to develop his own ambitions in the biggest one-day races," say the team.

UAE's Classics quad and transfer activity

UAE Team Emirates-XRG already have a strong squad for the Spring Classics and Gautherat will largely be deployed as a domestique.

Florian Vermeersch and Nils Politt have led the line in the cobbled Classics in the past couple of years, with the likes of Tim Wellens, Antonio Morgado, and Benoît Cosnefroy hopping in and out. Tadej Pogačar usually drops in for the Tour of Flanders – which he has now won three times – and Paris-Roubaix, which remains a gap and an itch in his other-worldly palmarès.

UAE Team Emirates-XRG have not made any major signings so far ahead of 2027. On the incomings list, Gautherat joins Marco Frigo from NSN Cycling, Abel Balderstone from Caja Rural, and Davide Stella from the team's development arm.

Perhaps their more significant pieces of business have been to tie Pogačar and Isaac del Toro to new long-term contract extensions.

On This Date in Knicks History: October 2
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Two noteworthy Knicks birthdays today!

Dr. Dick Barnett was born October 2, 1936, in Gary, Indiana. Barnett spent eight seasons with New York, became an All-Star in 1968, and played for both the 1970 and 1973 championship teams. His number 12 hangs in the Garden rafters. He died last year at 88.

Barnett had one of the most unforgettable shots in basketball history. Starting in college (when nicknamed “Dick the Skull”), he became known for contorting his body into a question mark while shooting his jumper, kicking his legs back and telling defenders, “Too late–fall back, baby!” Barnett went on to turn his eccentric shot into more than 15,000 NBA points.

A beloved teammate of Walt Frazier, Barnett was featured in the documentary film, , about his time playing at Tennessee State University for the Tigers. During segregation, the all-Black Tigers won three straight national championships. Captain Barnett tirelessly fought for their recognition, which culminated in their 2019 induction into the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame. Watch the doc here, you’ll dig it.

After hanging up his sneakers, Barnett earned an MBA from New York University and then a PhD in education from Fordham University. He taught Sports Management at St. John’s University for four years.

  • 2× NBA champion (1970, 1973)
  • All-ABL First Team (1962)
  • No. 12 retired by New York Knicks
  • 3× NAIA champion (1957–1959)
  • 3× AP Little College All-American (1957–1959)
  • 2× UPI Little College All-American (1958, 1959)
  • 2× NAIA tournament MVP (1958, 1959)

And (feeling like Garrison Keillor here) Tyson Chandler was born today in 1982, in Hanford, California. Chandler came to New York immediately after anchoring Dallas’ 2011 championship defense and became the 2011-12 NBA Defensive Player of the Year, the only Knick ever to take the honor.

Drafted second in 2001, the seven-foot Chandler played for five seasons in Chicago before bouncing from NOLA to Charlotte to Dallas and then the Knicks. After three seasons at MSG, he was sent back to Dallas, then Phoenix, and finished out his 19-year career with the Lakers and Rockets.

Chandler joined the Knicks in December 2011 via a sign-and-trade between multiple teams, which also sent traded Ronny Turiaf, cash, and a 2013 2nd-round draft pick to the Wizards. While there was no denying his talent, Chandler appeared on the injured list often during his tenure here, with a hamstring strain, playoff flu and an upper respiratory infection, a bulging cervical disc (plus related neck spasms and weight loss from illness), and a fractured right fibula.

In June 2014, he and Raymond Felton were traded to the Mavs for José Calderón, Samuel Dalembert, Wayne Ellington, Shane Larkin, a 2014 2nd-round draft pick (Thanasis Antetokounmpo was later selected), and a 2014 2nd-round draft pick (Cleanthony Early was later selected). (h/t basketball-reference.com)

Chandler concluded his time in New York with averages of 10.2 points, 10.1 rebounds, and 1.2 blocks across 183 games. His career highlights, also from Wikipedia:

  • All-NBA Third Team (2012)
  • NBA Defensive Player of the Year (2012)
  • NBA All-Defensive First Team (2013)
  • 2× NBA All-Defensive Second Team (2011, 2012)
  • First-team Parade All-American (2001)
  • Second-team Parade All-American (2000)
  • McDonald’s All-American (2001)
  • 2× California Mr. Basketball (2000, 2001)

Quite a nice pairing: two Knicks born 46 years apart, one remembered for his offense, the other for defense. Closing my Writer’s Almanac loop, your poem for the day is a personal favorite, “The Bear,” by Galway Kinnell.

Knicks in five. And keep in touch.

items.title: ‘That’s Ridiculous’: Team USA Captain Shoots Down Del Toro-McNulty Worlds Conspiracy
items.author: ahood
items.content: The controversy that won’t die: Warbasse and Creed tell Velo how Team USA’s bold tactics, not secret deals, put McNulty in the rainbow jersey.
items.lbText:
McNulty celebrates America's first world title in 33 years. (Photo: Tim de Waele/Getty Images)

Brandon McNulty had barely pulled on his rainbow jersey at the UCI Road World Championships before the internet goons started picking apart how he won it.

Tom Pidcock, perhaps frustrated at the finish line, threw the first barb, suggesting that Isaac del Toro helped his UAE teammate win the men’s road worlds in Montréal.

Then online sleuths found a clip of McNulty and Del Toro chatting at 36km to go, just a few kilometers before the Arizonan uncorked his winning move.

Team USA’s road captain laughed off the idea that Del Toro would throw away the world title to McNulty .

“No chance,” Warbasse told Velo . “I don’t think he was riding for Brandon. That’s just a bit ridiculous, obviously people are looking for storylines to build. To give it up? No way.”

In separate interviews with Velo , Warbasse and lead Team USA sports director Mike Creed picked apart cycling’s biggest viral conspiracy.

Creed countered that it was U.S. tactics that proved decisive, not some sort of deal hatched out on the road.

“It’s the tactic you learn when you’re juniors, use your teammates,” Creed said. “We’re just lucky we had three strong riders on really good days and we could do it.”

The UAE alliance theory just won’t die. Even nearly a week after the race, people are still debating it.

The final two laps of Sunday’s wild men’s worlds have been dissected more than the Zapruder film, with everyone seeing what they want to see about how McNulty stunned the favorites .

The fact that Team USA started with one of the strongest and most united teams in a worlds without the overwhelming favorite Tadej Pogačar doesn’t seem to matter.

“If Pogačar was there, everyone knew how the race would have gone,” Warbasse said in a telephone call with Velo . “We knew that if we wanted to get a result, we needed to try something a bit crazy.”

Del Toro, Paul Seixas with France, Mathieu van der Poel, and Belgium’s tandem of Wout van Aert and Remco Evenepoel were the big favorites.

The Americans were the ultimate underdogs.

Come crunch time, however, Team USA played their cards perfectly.

France had burned through its matches early, Del Toro was isolated and taking long pulls, and Belgium was all over the place. McNulty was waiting for his chance to pounce.

That famous video clip of McNulty and Del Toro chatting at 36km has became “magic bullet” for the supposed trade team alliance between the two UAE Emirates XRG teammates.

Warbasse just rolled his eyes when asked if he thought there was a pact in the making.

“I was chatting to my teammates also in the race, but that doesn’t mean that you’re working together,” Warbasse said. “If you’re next to your teammate, you’re probably like, damn, this is really hard, right?”

Creed made the same point , and nobody watching a clip knows what the two riders said.

“People do know that teammates will talk to each other during a race, right?” Creed told Velo . “Who knows what they said, maybe how hard the race is? He wasn’t about to give away the rainbow jersey.”

The awkward part of the theory is that it ignores everything Del Toro did trying to win the race himself.

Del Toro was racing like he wanted to win all day, even if the timing was a bit off sometimes.

But some point out the moment McNulty made his winning move with 32km to go, coming off the back of the group when Del Toro was at the front, and the Mexican didn’t immediately react.

Warbasse’s take is that Del Toro and Seixas took on too much responsibility too early, especially when Van der Poel went up the road with just over 90km to go.

And, like everyone else except the Americans, their legs were bien cuit going into the final decisive laps.

“I think both Del Toro and Seixas, they really assumed their roles of favorites, and they did a lot of work, probably a bit too much,” Warbasse said. “That really worked in our favor.”

With Quinn Simmons marking MVDP, their efforts played directly into American hands.

So when McNulty bolted, the favorites were already on their knees.

Velon posted a graphic on Instagram tracking the number of times the favorites accelerated over the final 100km.

Pidcock and Ben Healy topped the count with nine apiece, followed by Del Toro and Jorgenson with eight each. Van der Poel made six, while Giulio Ciccone and Seixas unloaded four each.

Jorgenson was covering moves. McNulty made one decisive acceleration that stuck.

Creed watched Del Toro taking repeated turns on the front. From his front-row seat in the lead U.S. team car, that hardly looked like a rider preparing to hand over a world title.

“I’m not going to go Alex Jones and put 90 clips online to make my case, but you don’t pull all day and then just give the race to McNulty,” Creed said. “If you just finished 270km and you’re frustrated, and your name is Tom Pidcock, that’s understandable.

“For everyone else, it’s just stirring the pot,” Creed said of the Del Toro-McNulty conspiracy. “I don’t know anyone who would give away the world championships.”

The Americans came into Montréal with three leaders: McNulty, Simmons, and Jorgenson, more than any squad in the elite men’s race.

That they finished with three in the top 10 — first, fourth, and eighth, respectively — shows how well the team raced.

“We were confident going in and we had probably one of the like strongest all-around teams, but maybe we just didn’t have that one like big name like a Remco or a Van der Poel,” Warbasse said.

Simmons circled Van der Poel as one to watch, so when the Dutchman attacked around 90km to go, Simmons was all over it.

With Simmons in front, McNulty and Jorgenson could sit on behind as their rivals did the work to pull back MVDP.

“So they were kind of able to get a free ride,” Warbasse said.

Creed described Simmons’ move as exactly what the Americans wanted. But getting a rider up the road only helps if he has the legs to stay there.…

items.title: Brandon McNulty's new world champion's bike is glittery, fun, and carries the torch from Tadej Pogačar's reign
items.author: william.jones@futurenet.com (Will Jones)
items.content:
Ever year a paint shop somewhere gets a call for a last minute paint job. White, with some rainbow details. The Colnago paint shop should be pretty well versed now, as Brandon McNulty has made it three years in a row for the men's world champion to be aboard the historic Italian brand.

While Tadej Pogačar started out his two-year reign as world champion on a white bike, he has raced on a black version ever since the middle of last season. And now, his teammate and heir McNulty, following his daring attack on the streets of Montreal last weekend, is carrying on that torch with a black, glittery Colnago Y1Rs that has just been unveiled.

Together, they are bucking the trend of white world champion's machines. Peter Sagan, Mark Cavendish, and at times Julian Alaphilippe all had black bikes, as did Anna Van der Breggen and Annamiek Van Vleuten in both of their separate stints as world champion. But in the last few years, white had come to dominate thanks to the likes of Mathieu van der Poel, Remco Evenepoel, and Lotte Kopecky.

As well as a difference in aesthetics, there's also a performance element in terms of weight; white paint usually uses heavy titanium-based pigments, and so opting for black is an easy way to shave grams.

According to Colnago, McNulty's new bike has a "glossy black carbon base enriched with a subtle glitter effect" and is "defined by a bold colour-block graphic featuring the iconic UCI rainbow stripes."

There's no denying the stripes, which make up the paint for the entirety of the forks as well as the majority of the rear triangle.

It's clearly a different look to what we've seen in recent seasons, and there is a fun easter egg hidden behind the bayonet fork hinge, as well as some trick upgrades that show that the focus has been on saving weight, meaning this is a bike that McNulty will actually be racing on, rather than simply shown off at sign-on before swapping to his more usual matte black version.

items.title: 'I wasn't confident at all' – Third time's a charm for Canadian sprinter Riley Pickrell as he takes first victory in over a year at Tour de Langkawi
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
How do you deal with a rider like Matteo Malucelli (XDS-Astana), who already has two stage victories at this year's Le Tour de Langkawi to add to his three stage wins in the preceding two editions?

"Go around him," was the response from Modern Adventure sports director Alex Howes when asked that exact question this morning in Pandan Indah, as the team never for a second appeared to have any doubt that Riley Pickrell could achieve the feat – not when the Canadian had been so closely matched with the XDS-Astana rider in the last two photo finish sprint stages.

"We think we're faster, so we've just got to show it," Howes told . And on stage 6 they certainly did.

There was no photo finish needed this time, with a stellar lead-out leaving Pickrell sheltering in the wheel of his last man, Scott McGill, until they had indeed gone around Malucelli and his lead-out, with just the job of finishing it off to complete.

After roaring in celebration over the line, the two-time runner-up, however, was taking nothing for granted.

"No, I wasn't confident at all," he said in response to a question from about his levels of certainty once he had got out in front with such a strong launch on the run to the line.

"The last two sprints, I was feeling really good, and then Malucelli came around me in the last three metres so I even did a bike throw on the line just to be sure. And the whole sprint, I was going, 'please don't come around me, please don't come around me, please don't come around me'," he said in a post-race interview with a small group of media.

This time, though, the result was clear. Pickrell had just taken his first win of the season on stage 6 of Le Tour de Langkawi, and he did it with his parents on the sidelines watching as they'd come all the way out to Malaysia to see him race. Plus, it was his first victory with the Modern Adventure squad and also the team's sixth win of its opening season, but first since June.

"The team has put a lot of a lot of trust in me this year and a lot of faith, and any day it doesn't work out, you're a little bit disappointed for yourself, and you're disappointed because your teammates have worked so hard for you and you didn't come away with the win," said Pickrell.

"And everyone knows it's part of the sport, but when you finally do get a win, it really feels like you're paying them back, and I can't be happier."

Though that doesn't mean he is going to lose focus on trying to do it all again in the next two sprint opportunities to come.

"I would say I walk away happy now, but I'm not going to walk away, and I'm always going to want more," said Pickrell.

*Cyclingnews attended Le Tour de Langkawi on an invitation/media package from the race that included travel and accommodation. items.title: Visma-Lease a Bike look to realise 'untapped potential' of British rider Mark Donovan as first new signing for 2027
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Visma-Lease a Bike have confirmed their first new signing for the 2027 season as Mark Donovan, with the British rider signing a two-year deal with the Dutch team.

Donovan, 27, will join after four seasons with Pinarello Q36.5, marking his first return to a WorldTour team since leaving DSM in 2022. A versatile climber and former GC winner of the Sibiu Tour in 2023, the Briton will bolster the team's climbing support.

"Visma-Lease a Bike is one of the best teams in the world, so when they come and ask you to join the team, there is no need to think twice," said Donovan on the team website.

"I’ve been in the professional peloton for quite some time now, and the past few years I’ve been able to develop and find out the type of rider I am, so making the step into this team really feels like the right moment for me, and I am really excited to see how much I can develop in this structure and which steps I will be able to take. While being part of a Grand Tour-winning team, I hope to be able to continue to show my consistency and hope to add my part in helping the team to win races."

Visma's most recent new arrival has been Fabio Jakobsen, but that was a mid-season transfer, with the Dutch rider and Picnic PostNL agreeing to terminate his contract early. The only other new rider confirmed as part of the 2027 roster is Matisse Van Kerckhove, who was announced to be stepping up from Visma's development team next season back in January.

Aside from being a consistent performer who should get through a mountain of work riding on the front in support of the super team's big leaders, Visma are also hoping to eke out some of his "untapped potential."

"I think Mark will fit very well into the way we approach racing. He has shown in recent seasons that he is a very reliable and versatile rider who can be relied upon in different situations, and he has the ability to perform when the level of the race is high," said Visma's head of racing Marc Reef.

"We see that being particularly valuable for us in stage races, where he can play an important role around our leaders. We also believe there is still some untapped potential that we are excited to develop together, as he is still only 27."

With Donovan's arrival and the majority of Visma's riders still being under contract into next year, their 2027 roster is already up to 28 riders. It comes after the shock retirement of Simon Yates in January and the imminent retirement of Steven Kruijswijk. The only 2026 rider on the team without a confirmed contract for next year at the Dutch team is Loe van Belle.

items.title: Russell says Red Bull strongest after Bahrain practice
items.content: <article>Red Bull are tipped by George Russell and Charles Leclerc as the team to beat after the first day at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.</article>
items.lbText:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen topped the timesheets as Formula 1 returned to the Sepang track for the first time in nine years for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Verstappen was 0.383 seconds quicker than George Russell, winner last week in Azerbaijan, in an upgraded Mercedes.

The second Red Bull of Isack Hadjar was third fastest, 0.783secs off the pace, ahead of Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, split from his team-mate Lewis Hamilton by championship leader Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes.

Alpine's Pierre Gasly was seventh fastest, ahead of the Racing Bulls of Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad, who will start from the back of the grid as a result of a grid penalty for using too many engine parts.

Hadjar also has a grid penalty - five places - for the same reason. And Alpine have changed Franco Colapinto's engine, giving him a 10-place penalty in addition to the five-place grid drop he was handed for causing a crash in the Azerbaijan Grand Prix last weekend.

F1 has returned to this track, regarded as one of the best layouts among the new generation of circuits that came on stream at the end of the last century and into this one, because of the circumstances around this year's calendar.

The Bahrain and Saudi Arabia races were cancelled at the beginning of the year as a result of the war in the Middle East.

But Bahrain were keen to hold their race and Crown Prince Salman bin Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa negotiated to hold the race in Malaysia.

A bunch of Bahraini-related activities are being held at the track, while the trophy presented will be the Bahrain Grand Prix trophy and rosewater rather than champagne will be sprayed on the podium.

The first session was marked by drivers commenting on the high level of tyre degradation caused by the abrasive surface, and Russell in particular noticed this was high on the Mercedes.

Questioning it on his race-simulation run late in the session, he was told his tyre wear did appear to be "an outlier" compared to that of Verstappen.

Mercedes have introduced their first major upgrade since the Canadian Grand Prix, with a new floor and rear bodywork.

They expected McLaren to be the team to beat at this track, but the world champions had a low-key first session, with Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris down in 11th and 12th places.

items.title: Belgian racers avoided World Championships disaster in run-in at US border, Alec Segaert reveals
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Belgium's men didn't have it all their own way at the Road World Championships this year as Remco Evenepoel and Wout van Aert missed out on the road race medals in Montreal. And it turns out that several of their teammates had a less than ideal week, too, encountering trouble at the US border before the race.

Speaking to the podcast, Alec Segaert, who raced to 11th in the time trial as Evenepoel took gold, recounted the troubles of Tiesj Benoot and Quinten Hermans at an American border post.

The pair had gone for a training ride from Belgium's base in Bromont, south-east of Montreal, towards the US border when they were stopped and reprimanded by American border officials.

"Those customs officers weren’t exactly laughing about it," Segaert said, according to . "They held them there for a few hours to fill out all sorts of paperwork. In the end, they didn’t ride another metre and were forced to return to Canada."

Regardless of their travails, Benoot and Hermans managed to complete a leg-aching 198km ride with 2,805 metres of climbing. Benoot uploaded the ride to Strava, jokingly naming it 'Mexico was in sight'.

The map of the ride shows the route the pair took towards the border, heading due south from Belgium's base, before turning around and heading on their ultra-long training loop back north.

"It was a very small border post, where very few cars passed in those 2 to 3 hours. In any case, they were definitely not allowed through on bicycles. Checks had to be carried out to see if they weren't members of cartels or something similar," Segaert said.

In the end, Benoot and Hermans avoided any cases of mistaken identity and got back to base to continue preparations for the race. Benoot rode to 25th place on the 273km course as Hermans recorded a DNF.

items.title: The hidden potential in Honda's home MotoGP weekend
Luka Mezgec announces new role as sports director at top WorldTour team following imminent retirement after European Championships
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
Just weeks after his imminent retirement on Sunday at the European Road Championships, Slovenian veteran racer Luka Mezgec is set to join Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe as a sports director.

Appropriately enough for a rider best-known for his sprinting and leadout work during a 17- year career, Mezgec will waste no time at all heading to the German WorldTour squad, where he'll begin work.

After breaking the news on the Slovenian radio station, , Mezgec told specialist sports website that one of the main missions in his new job will be working with young Italian sprinter Alessio Magagnotti.

"For some time now, I have had the desire to remain in cycling as a sports director after my career ends. In the end, I had three options, and of these, Red Bull-Bora-hansgrohe seemed the most interesting," Mezgec, who signed his contract with Red Bull during the 2026 Tour, told Sportal.

"Alessio is a very young sprinter who will move from the development team to the pros next year, and I can offer him all the experience I have gained over the years as a sprinter and later as a lead-out man."

Set to meet with his new team just a few weeks away, Mezgec explained it would be difficult for him to have a role working with the GC challengers in the squad, because it was so far outside his own knowledge.

As he wryly put it, "I don't know what it's like if there are three of us left at the end of the race; I only know what it's like if there's a bunch. It would be difficult for me to explain things that I've never experienced myself.

"But I know what it's like in the bunch, how the preparation for a sprint works and what a sprinter needs. I can pass on these experiences to him."
