items.title: From elbow surgery to fighting for victory in a matter of days – Just starting Tour de Langkawi 'a bit of a bonus' for Josh Burnett
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
It was a strong performance for the rider from New Zealand in any circumstances – but even more so given a week ago he wasn't even sure he would be able to take to the start line.

"Two days before the race, a car pulled out on us, and I had to have overnight surgery to repair my elbow. So yeah, for me, being on the start line was a bit of a bonus, so then to do what I did yesterday…" Burnett told on Friday at the start of stage 6 in Pandan Indah.

"To move up into seventh overall and take second on such a cool stage is amazing, and everyone saw the crowds up there. It was pretty epic to be at the front of that."

Burnett explained that the midnight surgery for a "severe cleaning" of the big wound of his arm had taken a toll in the earlier stages but stage 5 was one, which finished with a long climb in the Genting Highlands, that he had earmarked as a good opportunity even before he arrived in Malaysia.

The plan, however, hadn't initially been to go in the break but it took some time to establish and strong riders were persistent in continuing the effort so Burnett and his Burgos Burpellet-BH teammate Rodrigo Alvarez joined the fray. Along with some others a strong duo of TotalEnergies riders also joined the fray, Nicolas Breuillard and Valentin Retailleau. This helped give the break plenty of horsepower.

"Initially, I was a bit hesitant when I was in there, but when the gap started going out, I started to believe slowly and slowly a bit more," said Burnett.

Five minutes advantage at the bottom of the climb, also meant Burnett was the virtual leader of the race on the road as he was the best-placed rider out the front, in 17th at 3:20 from race leader Lennart Jasch (Tudor Pro Cycling).

The pressure of the climb cut the break down to just Breuillard and Burnett, with the rider from New Zealand working hard to keep driving the pace, thinking about not just the stage but also the overall. However, at 2.6km to go the French rider accelerated and at that point, Burnett just couldn't respond.

"Honestly, I felt really good and maybe a bit stronger but I had to ride for the GC, so I did most of the work, and then I just kind of cramped when he went. I knew if I tried to follow it would have been both legs that would have stopped working," said Burnett. "The cramps kind of went away, and I maybe closed it a few seconds, but obviously I never really got that close but I tried and TotalEnergies worked just as hard as us so they deserved it as well."

In the end Burnett was second with an eight second gap to Breuillard and with Jasch having delivered yet another strong showing on the climb he well and truly kept his race lead safe and took third on the stage just 13 seconds back from Burnett.

And while the Burgos Burpellet BH rider was not, in the end, a threat to Jasch, he did deliver a reshuffling further back in the top 10, moving up ten spots to seventh overall.

"Obviously, when you're here, you want a bit more, but when you look at it objectively, I think it's pretty good for sure," said Burnett, who then went on to prove just how big the lure of more is as he attempted to make the break once again on stage 6.

items.title: Why Verstappen and Hadjar urge Red Bull to "make all the mistakes now" for 2027
'I'm getting better each day after the crash' – Tadej Pogačar provides injury update at 2031 World Championships presentation
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Speaking at the presentation of the 'Super' 2031 UCI World Championships in Trentino, Pogačar dialled in via video call and said he's been "getting better every day after the crash."

He's not been completely keeping away from the cycling world either, confirming he had been watching the Worlds, where UAE Team Emirates-XRG teammate Brandon McNulty took solo victory for the USA. After the win on Sunday, Pogačar hailed him as "the King of Montreal."

"I'm very well, thanks. I'm getting better each day after the crash. I'm back riding my bike, and I'm enjoying the nice autumn days here in Slovenia," said Pogačar.

"Yes, of course. In the final, I was definitely rooting for a few people, and one of them was Brandon, for sure, so it was such a hectic race, and in the end Brandon crossed the line, and I could not believe he did it. I was so, so happy for him. Then we spoke the next day, and it was a really special moment."

Two-time road race World Champion Pogačar should return to the World Championships in 2027 in Haute-Savoie, the next 'Super' Worlds after Glasgow in 2023. But he is also hoping to be still racing by the time the 2031 event rolls around.

"I hope I will be there racing. It's my dream to still be good then. But I'm not getting younger, so for sure there are going to be many, many competitors for these World Championships, maybe that I don't even know yet, and every year is going to be harder," said Pogačar.

"But it doesn't matter; I look forward to being there in 2031 at this Super World Championship and to being able to compete in the beautiful Trentino. I'll give my best if I have the chance."

For the moment, though, as his condition continues to improve, the sport's time rider will only be seen on his bike in training alongside Žigart, with his UAE team confirming that a return to the Europeans or Il Lombardia later this month is still too soon.

"We go out on the bike almost every day together; obviously we have different training plans," said the Slovenian.

"But for example, the last few days, she's definitely been beating my ass on the climbs and the downhills as well, so I'm following her lead now, and we have a good time on the bike together."

items.title: Taylor Phinney Keeps Olympic Dream Alive with First Track Worlds in 16 Years
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Phinney, Kristen Faulkner, Ashlin Barry lead USA at UCI track world championships as Phinney chases fairytale Olympic comeback in LA.
items.lbText:
Taylor Phinney is heading back to track worlds (Photo: Tim Ireland/PA Images/ Getty Images)

Taylor Phinney , Kristen Faulkner , and Ashlin Barry headline Team USA’s selection for the track world championships in Shanghai this month.

The U.S. is sending a deep 17-rider roster to China as USA Cycling looks to build off of the back of unprecedented double-gold success at the recent road worlds in Montréal.

The 19-year-old Barry – who stampeded to solo victory at the U23 road race in Montréal last weekend – is joined by the 36-year-old Phinney in the seven-man endurance squad.

Faulkner leads the women’s team after she finished 21st in both the road race and TT in Montréal. The 33-year-old Olympic and PanAm track champion is joined by five more women on the U.S. endurance team.

USA Cycling is also sending four women to the sprint events after the team recorded a best-ever worlds finish last year in Santiago, Chile.

Phinney’s selection to the worlds team will stoke his dream of making a fairytale return to the Olympic Games.

The Coloradan came out of competitive retirement this spring with the sole mission of making it to L.A. 2028.

Phinney hasn’t raced track worlds since 2010, when he won the individual pursuit and hit the podium in the omnium. However, after winning gold in the U.S. national team pursuit this summer, it’s not out of the question that Phinney adds to a track worlds trophy collection that’s been gathering dust for 16 years.

The UCI track world championships run from October 14 through 18 in Shanghai, China.

items.title: UEC European Championships: Mara Winter shocks the WorldTour favourites to claim women's under-23 title in tight finish
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Mara Winter (Switzerland) pulled off a huge ride to crown herself European champion, seeing off a quality four-woman group that included the world champion to win the U23 women’s road race at the 2026 European Championships.

But Winter, who rides at Continental level for the Nexetis team, boldly took control of the sprint, leading it out from the front and holding off the others despite the long-range effort.

Vinke was the runner-up, a wheel shy, with Chladoňová taking the bronze medal ahead of Arens.

"I can’t believe it, I think I’m dreaming," said Winter.

"To be honest, I did not dare to dream about it. I don’t know what to say. I never expected this and I never allowed myself to dream about this. It’s such a huge thing. I can’t believe it."

The U23 women’s road race was the opener of these European Championships in Slovenia, and while it measured just 88.4 kilometres, it actually contained more elevation gain than the 130km elite women’s race to come on Saturday. That’s because it was based exclusively on the finishing circuit of these Championships, with the Možjanca climb – 2.1km at 10.2% – covered four times.

The Dutch took control from the start, and while the first two ascents were whittling-down and softening-up processes, the race really opened up on the third ascent. Winter was front and centre, going clear in the company of Arens, the junior time trial world champion from last year.

On the fourth and final ascent of Možjanca, Chladoňová and Vienke went clear of the rest of the vastly-reduced chase group and steadily worked their way across to Winter and Arens on the steep gradients. They hadn’t even made contact when Vienke launched a big attack, which was followed by another move from Arens nearer the top, but they crested together as a quartet, and rode over the plateau and down the descent into the finale.

Any room for tactical manouevre for the Dutch, however, was threatened by the six-woman chase group that emerged on the climb and that ate into the gap in the latter phases. With around 7km to go it was 30 seconds but they closed to within 10 seconds at 4km to go. The front group had to work well together to keep them at bay, and the sting went out of the chase with 2km to go, leaving the front four to fight it out in a sprint.

Chladoňová moved her way to the front, but Winter boldly pushed her way into the lead for the final right-hand bend with 500 metres to go. She took pole position, but looked like something of a sitting duck with the others in her wheel and a long way to the line. Remarkably, however, she wound up her speed and held off her increasingly desperate rivals for a brilliant victory and a major title.

items.title: 'I would be probably just cracking a top 20' – Chris Froome talks Tadej Pogačar, the state of modern cycling, and his years in the wilderness post-injury
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
It might be only a year since Chris Froome retired, but it’s more than eight years since his most recent win, so it’s easy to forget how he once dominated the Grand Tours. He won seven three-week races in the eight seasons between 2011 and 2018, as well as the Critérium du Dauphiné three times and the Tour de Romandie twice. For a long stretch of the 2010s he was the sport’s best stage racer, bar none.

Despite that success and status, it’s surprising how little we’ve heard from the now-41-year-old in recent years. Yes, his career tailed off without a single victory after he joined Israel-Premier Tech in 2021, and the 2025 crash which ended his career a few months prematurely drew attention, but he was too busy recovering from life-threatening injuries to be speaking to the press. But other than a couple of interviews at the Tour de France last year, where he was working as an ambassador for Škoda, there’s been little else until the last couple of weeks.

Doing brand ambassador work, as well as investing in a few cycling companies, is how Froome spends a lot of his time now. It's at an event for two of these brands – a joint Ekoï and Factor ride-out in south-west London – that is reunited with the four-time Tour de France winner, the leafy Surrey Hills a far-cry away from the mountains of France and the intensity of his racing career.

"Your absolute goal is to get to that point where you can drive your opponents to think that they're only racing for second place."

Socalising before the ride, there’s a hint he likes life away from the spotlight. He's relaxed, smiling and chatting with the other guests as if he was just any other cyclist. Other than his colourful and flashy Factor One bike – a brand he's a shareholder in – he’s no different on the road:the smiles, photos and chattiness continue, and he even pushes one of the slower punters up some of the climbs. He might be the star of the show, but for all intents and purposes, he’s just one of the group today.

"I’m trying to get out once or twice a week at least," he tells after the ride. "Just with friends, keeping it social, or pro riders who are on their recovery days – I wouldn't dare go with them on a normal training day anymore. That chapter is firmly closed for me, no temptation to want to get back into any competitive kind of racing or anything."

Such is his low-key persona and the passing of time it’s easy for to forget that he was to the 2010s what Tadej Pogačar is to the 2020s, and for now at least he has more Grand Tour wins than the Slovenian. However, Froome is the first to baulk at the comparison.

Tadej Pogačar is 'writing his own history', says Froome

"What he's doing is just is just phenomenal, nothing but admiration and respect," Froome says of his Slovenian successor, winning many of the things Froome used to win, albeit in a totally different way and indeed era.

"What he's doing is not rewriting history, but he's writing his own history in the sport. When the level is so high already, and the margins between everyone else are so slim he's able to be head and shoulders above everyone else. What he's doing in Classics is probably even more impressive to me than what he's doing in the Grand Tours.

"I understand what training it took to be ready for races like the Tour de France or Vuelta and Giro, but I would write myself off from being competitive in one-day races. I understood that they're almost like two different sports. So how he's able to do both and literally just go from February until October at that level is…"

Froome tails off before modestly admitting that, like Pogačar, he too dominated the sport, and while he understands how fans might find such dominance boring, he doesn’t.

"We’re witnessing something very special, and it's a pleasure to watch him race. It must be extremely demoralising for his competitors, but as a bike rider, this is what you strive to become.

"I had huge respect for that, that that is 100% what I would try and do. First mountain top finish lay down the law, absolutely blow them away, and mentally you've already won the race. So, yeah, I would very much make that my goal in a lot of lot of these races."

Froome might come across as mild-mannered, but in talking about Pogačar he offered an insight into the mentality which made him the Grand Tour great he was, but where would he be now?

"No, no, no, there's no question. I would be probably just cracking a top 20 in the race now, even though it's only six, seven years on from when I was winning," he says with a rueful smile, citing improvements in tyres, bikes and aerodynamics, but emphasising nutrition.

"When I was winning the Tour de France we were probably fuelling not more than about 40-50 grams [of carbohydrates] an hour, and now it's over over 100, 150 at times on the big stages. We're not talking about a 20, 30% increase in fuelling, we’re talking about a 300% increase."

While Froome experienced plenty of success through his career, it was punctuated by two very serious crashes. Just last year, weeks before what should have been his final race, he crashed while on a training ride, suffering multiple internal injuries, ending his career, and in 2019 he lost control of his bike while sighting the Critérium du Dauphiné time trial. As a result he knows something of how Pogačar might feel after his crash on stage 8 of the recent Vuelta a España, which ended the UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider’s race and season.

"I think it’s really personal," he says. "Thankfully for him, it wasn't his error, it was one of those fluke accidents, so I wouldn't imagine there would be any reason for him to have any fear after this. Some guys just have to see someone else crashing and they’ll have fear for months down the line.

"I was incredibly fortunate that after my 2019 crash, when I broke my leg in two places, that I didn't have that fear. But I also don't remember my crash, it was just erased from my memory, I must have hit my head hard enough, or it was enough of a shock that I don't remember the crash at all. [Otherwise] I’d be always second guessing myself, going into corners at high speed, thinking, 'What if I mess this one up like I did before?’"

That crash in June 2019 saw him not only forced out of that year’s Tour de France, but it also marked the end of his career as a winner. He returned to racing the following February but failed to bag even a top 10 finish throughout 2020, his final season with what was by then Ineos Grenadiers.

A move to Israel-Premier Tech proved no more successful, though he came oh so close to winning on Alpe d’Huez during the 2022 Tour de France, eventually finishing third behind a rampant Tom Pidcock, a result he describes as good as a win. While he managed second place in the team time trial at the 2024 Tour du Rwanda, that day on the Alpe was the last individual top 10 placing of his career, and the man who had once been the greatest Grand Tour rider of his generation faded away, his team boss Sylvan Adams branding him as 'not value for money'. But Froome sees it from his own perspective.

"I just felt so fortunate to be able to come back to the sport I love doing. I got into the sport quite late and I made it a goal to be racing into my 40s, and I don't think anyone understood at the age of 36, when I had a big crash, why I would want to come back.

"I honestly felt that had I not continued on and really given it everything I had to see if I could come back and win a fifth Tour de France, I would probably have spent the rest of my life questioning," he says, speaking more hesitantly, emotion clear.

"I can now retire satisfied that I did everything I could. It's no longer a question in my mind. What if? What if? What if? I know. I did it. I realised I wasn't able to get back to that level. That the level had changed. It wasn't the same level as it was pre-crash.

"But I think it took a good two and a half, three years of chasing it for it to really sink in, that level where I was previously has changed, the sport’s moved on. But I think my competitive career honestly ended when I hit that wall in 2019."

Back in the Surrey Hills, there might be some steep gradients and even some gravel on the lanes, but it's a far cry from the Colle delle Finestre where Froome took the final win of his career, more than seven years before he finally retired. There, during the 2018 Giro d'Italia, he memorably obliterated the competition, in the pre-Pogačar era, his attack was barely conceivable, planting confusion among his rivals and completing the then Team Sky rider's Grand Tour clean sweep.

"The one single, best day on the bike, hands down," Froome asserts. "I think there was never one day that won me the Grand Tour like that did. I was almost four minutes down in GC, just rolling the dice and banking on something happening behind me, that they wouldn't have collusion in chasing.

"I knew that my team had set a hard enough tempo on the Colle delle Finestre that people wouldn't have domestiques left. So it would be between the rest of the guys who were up there on GC, who was going to pull, who was going to take responsibility, and it just so happened to work in my favour that they were kind of bickering amongst themselves. They had Carapaz and Amador sitting on, not pulling through. It was basically Pinot and Dumoulin doing all the work, and they probably were in a very negative mindset chasing me, whereas I was out front and I was just having the day of my life."

items.title: No Pogačar, All the Pressure: Evenepoel Riding For Redemption after Worlds Washout
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: 'Inexplicably bad': Evenepoel needs to reset the narrative Sunday at European championships as Vollering and Niewiadoma brace for titan battle in women's.
items.lbText:
No Tadej Pogačar, no Paul Seixas, no Tom Pidcock: The European championship road race should be a walk in the park for Remco Evenepoel on Sunday.

Anything less than victory would be a catastrophe.

That’s the message churning up the Belgian media as the bike-mad nation picks over the debris of what’s been treated as a sporting disaster.

After starting last Sunday’s world championship road race as the team to beat , the Belgians were bullied by Team USA’s powershow in Montréal.

Evenepoel in 12th, Wout van Aert in 28th.

There’s been a Belgian public inquest ever since.

“They all failed,” fumed Belgian pro-turned-pundit Jans Bakelants as he dissected his home team’s performance in HLN .

“I find it inexplicable that they were all so bad,” he raged.

Evenepoel faced an online flagellation after he admitted he “just wasn’t good enough” in Montréal.

The Belgian dailies are still debating roster selections and speculating over a team sickness after Sunday’s worlds washout.

Evenepoel’s historic fourth consecutive world time trial title and standout podium finish at the Tour de France were forgotten about.

Evenepoel can rapidly reset the narrative Sunday at Slovenia’s European championship road race.

He’s a tier above the rest of a start list weakened by fatigue, impoverished national federations, and straight-up apathy to a championship few seem to care about.

In fact, the one rider who does really care about this year’s Euros won’t even be racing.

Pogačar is a confirmed non-starter for his “home” race Sunday after this week’s “ will-he-won’t-he ” confab.

Meanwhile, Seixas is saving his legs for Il Lombardia, Pidcock’s British team chose to focus only on the TTs, and Mattias Skjelmose is out sick.

So who does Remco have to beat to reprise his curious new celebration and put the wheels back on his best season yet at the European championships?

Primož Roglič, Juan Ayuso, and Giulio Ciccone are Remco’s main rivals for the 196km race across Pogačar’s home turf.

Victory on Sunday would complete Evenepoel’s set of road titles, having already won the Olympic, world, and Belgian races. It would trampoline him toward an end-of-season showdown with Seixas and Isaac del Toro at Il Lombardia.

But even then, some might see it as a consolation prize.

The women’s European road race on Saturday should be a thriller that more than offsets any potential one-man show on Sunday.

Demi Vollering and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney will lock in for a third round of their battle royale in Saturday’s championships after they went 1-2 at both the Tour de France Femmes and road worlds.

Hot off a world title victory, Vollering is in prime position to defend her European title in Slovenia and earn a blue-and-white jersey she’ll never wear.

Niewiadoma proved in Montréal she won’t let Vollering have it easy.

Elisa Longo Borghini, Paula Blasi, Marlen Reusser, and Franziska Koch lead the opposition to the two women who have dominated this summer of cycling.

Both the men’s and women’s road races this weekend will be decided by the nasty ramps of the Mozjanca climb.

The women climb the 2.1km, 10% kicker twice in the back-half of their 130km race. The men take it on five times in their 196km race.

The women’s and men’s time trials take place on Wednesday, October 7.

Riders to watch: Vollering (Netherlands), Niewiadoma-Phinney (Poland), Longo-Borghini (Italy), Reusser (Switzerland), Blasi (Spain), Koch (Germany).

Riders to watch: Evenepoel (Belgium), Roglič (Slovenia), Ciccone, Pellizzari (both Italy), Ayuso (Spain), Pedersen (Denmark).

items.title: How Brandon McNulty’s Unconventional Training Plan Made Him a World Champion
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: High heat over altitude, and intensity over volume. Here are the details behind the training blocks that powered McNulty ahead of the world's best.
items.lbText:
(Photo: Zac Williams - Pool/Getty Images)

Brandon McNulty is a unique rider in more ways than one. Not only did he become the first American to win the elite road race at the 2026 UCI Road World Championships in more than 30 years, but he is also a rider who never goes to altitude camps. The Arizonan rides alongside Tadej Pogačar at the Tour de France, but instead of living on a mountain a month before the Tour, he is more often at home, training at 5:00 a.m. in the desert.

When McNulty lined up for the World Championships in Montreal, many considered him an outsider with a chance at a medal, but few thought that he had the capacity to win. The 28-year-old hadn’t won a race in the entire 2026 season, which was quite concerning after he rounded out the 2025 season by winning six races in two months, including the WorldTour-level Tour de Pologne and Grand Prix Cycliste de Montréal.

Whatever happened in the 2025/2026 off-season remains a bit of a mystery, yet McNulty started the year with a few top-five finishes in February. After a DNF at Paris-Nice, McNulty was solid again in April before taking a short break pre-Tour de Suisse. The American showed good form while helping Pogačar, but he was still never in the top five throughout the entire race. His best finish at the Tour was fifth place on a breakaway stage, and the rest of his time in France was spent helping Pogačar.

McNulty’s results were nothing to write home about, so few considered him as a worlds favorite. But between his DNF on Stage 18 of the Tour de France on July 23 and winning the World Championships on September 27, something changed. This is how Brandon McNulty trained to win the rainbow jersey.

There were exactly 66 days between July 23 and September 27, which means that McNulty had nine and a half weeks to go from abandoning the Tour to winning worlds. First, he took 10 days off the bike. That is a long break in the middle of the season, but in hindsight, it was the perfect amount of time. McNulty then returned to training with five consecutive easy rides — that means Zone 1 and Zone 2, without intervals or any additional stress. He was riding 2-3 hours a day, not the 5-6 daily hours that you might expect from other professional cyclists.

His first workout post-Tour de France was a classic UAE Team Emirates session: four-minute torque intervals. We’ll see these a lot in McNulty’s training plan, and they are much harder than they look. In this post-Tour workout, McNulty did 7x4min at 45 rpm, getting up to a max heart rate of ~170 bpm at the end of each interval. Knowing McNulty’s heart rate zones and history, we can assume these intervals were done at threshold power, which is likely around 450w for McNulty.

Workout #1: 4-minute torque intervals (45 rpm) at 100% FTP

The day after this torque workout, McNulty completed 3x30min intervals with a heart rate of 155-165bpm during each 30min block. That means he was probably riding at Tempo, or Zone 3. McNulty said that he climbed the Voie Camillien-Houde in Zone 2 on the final lap of the World Championships, and by my calculations, McNulty’s Zone 2 is approximately 5.3w/kg, or 365w. That means these Tempo intervals are likely done at 380-400w, making for an interval session like this isn’t the toughest, but it’s crucial to get accustomed to riding at this pace for extended periods of time, especially when you are training to win races solo.

One of the key principles of McNulty’s training plan is progressive overload, and that’s exactly what we saw with his first ride five weeks out from worlds. The American did 3x35min Tempo at 145-155 bpm, up from 3x30min the week before. The same principle applies to the short torque intervals, which now added a 30-second sprint at the end of each interval. McNulty also completed an additional rep, which meant this week’s workout was 8x4min Torque intervals (45 rpm) at 100% FTP straight into a 30-second sprint.

After a few days of Zone 2 and recovery riding, McNulty went out for a two-hour endurance ride on Friday, but this one was different. Twenty minutes after he got home, McNulty was on the trainer for an hour with his heart rate rising from 130 bpm to 170 bpm by the end of the session. It’s extremely likely that this was a heat training session, something that McNulty and so many other pros have been utilizing before key races each season. The following day included the same style of Tempo intervals that we’ve already seen, but this time they were 40 minutes each.

The following day included a new workout in this block of training: 3x10min 30/30s from 160-170 bpm. Since McNulty is only hitting 90% of his max heart rate, my best guess is that these 30/30s are done just below and just above threshold. For McNulty, this could be something like: 30 seconds at 420w followed by 30 seconds at 470w.

Next up was another threshold interval session, but this time with much longer blocks. This workout was 2x20min over/unders with one minute VO2 Max followed by four minutes just under threshold. Intervals like these are designed to train your body to clear lactate, even at a high power output. The days of 2x20min at FTP are gone; almost every modern-day pro is doing over/unders instead.

At the end of this training week, McNulty did his worlds prep session: 6x4min VO2 Max and 6x30sec sprints. This is an incredibly hard workout, but one that McNulty uses to get into race shape. Not only are the VO2 Max intervals challenging, but the sheer number of efforts in this workout is a true challenge of fatigue resistance. Doing a fresh 30-second sprint is one thing; now try doing 30 seconds all-out after spending 24 minutes in your VO2 Max zone and sprinting five times full gas. These are the kinds of workouts that give McNulty the ability to attack four hours deep into a hard race.…

items.title: F1 Bahrain GP in Malaysia: Verstappen pips Russell to top FP1
Ferguson 'terrified' before 'fantastic' return to Man Utd after brain haemorrhage
items.content: <article>Former Manchester United manager Sir Alex Ferguson speaks to BBC Breakfast as he approaches his 85th birthday.</article>
items.lbText:
"I was terrified," says Sir Alex Ferguson, one of the fiercest, most explosive and most decorated managers in football history.

The legendary former Manchester United boss is recalling the day he returned to Old Trafford for the first time after suffering a brain haemorrhage in May 2018.

Four months after emergency surgery, Ferguson - famous for his 'hairdryer treatment' when United dominated English football - was back to watch his beloved club take on Wolves in the Premier League.

The man responsible for making the dreams of United fans around the world come true for once was unsure of the reception he would receive from supporters.

"I wish I could say I was comfortable. I wasn't," Ferguson tells BBC Breakfast.

Ferguson and his wife Cathy received a standing ovation when they took their seats in the directors' box before kick-off.

"My wife was with me, and she was nearly crying," he said. "When we sat down, she said: 'That's fantastic.'"

Ferguson had been retired five years - after winning 38 trophies during 26 years in charge of United - at the time of his brain haemorrhage, aged 76.

Now three months short of 85, he says: "I'm feeling quite good despite small injuries."

The Scot has a new book coming out - 'Games of My Life'. It tells the stories of 21 defining matches in his playing and managerial career, revealing fresh insights into his journey from working-class Glasgow to dominating the English game - and Europe - as United boss.

Ferguson is thankful he is able to talk about the games that helped shape him.

"I had lost my voice; I couldn't speak," he says about the days immediately after brain surgery. "That was a frightening moment.

"I remember my grandsons coming to see me and I had lost my voice.

"Then they brought in a therapist and she started doing things like asking me to write down the names of birds, names of animals, names of rivers.

Unseen pictures in new Sir Alex Ferguson book detailing his favourite games

Ferguson won the lot during his time in charge of United between 1986 and 2013, including 13 Premier League titles.

He transformed them into a winning machine, and the history and tradition of United ran red through his veins.

As well as delivering two Champions League titles, Ferguson masterminded five FA Cup triumphs, won the League Cup four times and added the Club World Cup, European Super Cup, European Cup Winners' Cup and the Intercontinental Cup to the Old Trafford trophy cabinet.

In his book, Ferguson has picked standout games in his career, from winning his first cup final playing for Govan High School in Glasgow in 1955 at the age of 13 through to his retirement as a manager in 2013.

"That was my starting point," he says, holding the medal he received after that cup win 71 years ago.

"I played for Glasgow Schools, Scotland Schools and the Scotland youth team. The starting point of my career was there and I can look back with great satisfaction."

Ferguson describes growing up in Govan as "the making of me". He says he developed his inner confidence from his mother Elizabeth and a drive to succeed from his father Alexander, who worked in the Govan shipyards on the River Clyde.

"He was so proud of me and my brother," says Ferguson.

"He was a hard taskmaster because whenever I scored a hat-trick or a goal, my mother would say 'that's great, son'." His father, meanwhile, offered tough constructive criticism however many goals Ferguson had scored.

After making his debut as a 16-year-old striker for Queen's Park, Ferguson ended up at St Johnstone, where he endured a frustrating spell and nearly quit football for a new life in Canada.

"I wasn't enjoying it. I wasn't playing first-team football; I was in the reserves all the time," he says.

"I filled out all the forms and phoned my aunt in Canada, because you needed a sponsor then, and never told my mother and father."

The next day St Johnstone, decimated by a flu bug in the team, arrived at Ibrox to take on Rangers. A 21-year-old Ferguson was promoted to the starting XI and scored a hat-trick.

That life-changing performance in 1963 revived his playing career and set him on the path to becoming one of football's greatest managers.

"I would say this to young people - don't miss the biggest opportunity in your life. It's recognising it."

Ferguson is sat in front of a table for the interview, which was conducted before the Premier League announced on Tuesday that Manchester City had been found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of financial regulations between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

On the table are several items from his career, including the Scotland cap he was finally presented with in 2021 - 54 years after appearing for his country.

Ferguson received the cap at Hampden Park on the night Scott McTominay - then a United player - scored a dramatic stoppage-time winner in a 3-2 win over Israel in a World Cup qualifier.

"I remember signing McTominay at seven years of age," Ferguson says.

Also on the table are old letters addressed to Ferguson from disgruntled United fans amid speculation he was about to sell midfielder Paul Ince to Inter Milan in the summer of 1995.

One reads: 'Don't sell Incey to Inter - or you'll regret it'. Another reads: 'Every Red is disgusted with you'.

"Paul was a tremendous footballer, there's no doubt about that," says Ferguson.

"He had incredible ability, but I just had that feeling that he just got carried away a bit at the time.

"He then got this offer from Inter Milan. I'm trying to weigh up one thing against the other. I'm looking at Paul Scholes and I said 'should we?'

"Milan's offer went from £7m to £7.5m and I said 'do it'.

"That's what your job is as a manager. You have to make hard decisions, and some decisions don't suit everyone."

There is also a notebook on the table with a list of words scribbled down by Ferguson when he used to address his players.…

items.title: Riley Pickrell gets his Le Tour de Langkawi sprint win on stage 6 with Matteo Malucelli second
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
After two runner-up spots, Riley Pickrell (Modern Adventure) snared his Le Tour de Langkawi victory on stage 6, managing to get the better of Matteo Malucelli (XDS-Astana) by taking out the short and sharp day of racing from Pandan Indah to Rembau.

It was a clear-cut win this time, no need to wait for the photo finish to celebrate, as the Canadian and his team played the slightly uphill finish to perfection. Seppe Van Den Boer (Tudor Pro Cycling) made it to the podium again, with the 20-year-old taking third place on the 121.3km stage that offered the third sprint opportunity of the race.

"The last two sprints it was pretty clear that Malucelli and me are super close and the only reason I won today was that the boys put me in a better position than Malucelli's boys. But that's just the nature of bike racing, and I can't thank my team enough," said Pickrell in a post-race interview.

"We knew we had to be in a really good position and we were hoping my teammate Scott [McGill] could drop me off just before the corner, but he had really good legs, so he was able to take me through the corner. He gave me a really good run to the finish and I'm really happy."

Race leader Lennart Jasch (Tudor Pro Cycling) maintained his top spot overall, sitting 26 seconds ahead of Alex Balderstone (Caja Rural-Seguros RGA) with two more flat stages ahead.

Still, even though the race ended in a sprint and with the GC gap holding firm, it certainly wasn't a relaxing day defending the jersey for Jasch, with plenty of moves early, which meant the first-year pro had to stay on his toes.

There was no easing into this early-starting stage, which launched at 9am local time, as it was possibly the best opportunity for riders trying to capitalise on a break and thwart the sprinters' teams, who had been in energy-conservation mode through the mountain stages. It also offered a chance for others to make up some ground in the overall.

This was because, even though the big summit finishes were in the past, the climbs were not completely in the rear-view mirror. The first category 3 climb at Ampang came at just 5km into the day of racing and then another at Bukit Hantu at 18km.

Over the first climb, Petr Rikunov (Wheeltop Rotor Chengdu) looked to build points in hopes of returning to the top of the KOM classification where he started the day second to Jasch. The race leader was next, clearly wary of the threat to the leader's orange jersey the hectic opening run on this stage could pose.

There were in fact early splits in the peloton, with the winner of two stages so far, Matteo Malucelli (XDS-Astana), among those off the back after he and a teammate had a flat at one of the worst possible moments, while Stefan de Bod (Modern Adventure) was off the front between the two early climbs. It bunched up in the peloton through the second, then Mathias Bregnhøj (Terengganu), sitting eighth overall and Josh Burnett (Burgos-Burpellet BH), who, after his second place on stage 5, is seventh overall, made a move, but Jasch wasn't letting a pair who posed such a GC threat get away, chasing the move himself.

Bregnhøj had another go with Matthis Le Berre (TotalEnergies), but they were also pulled back in. The group that finally established included Alan Jousseaume (TotalEnergies), Julien Arriola (Caja Rural-Seguros RGA) and Adne van Engelen (Terengganu), who were later also joined by Juan Martinez (Picnic PostNL), Mikel Retegi (Equipo Kern Pharma) and Rikunov, who took the top KOM points at 66km into the day of racing.

The peloton was back together behind, which meant that with their in-form sprinter in the fold, XDS-Astana were now prepared to go to the front and try to reel in the lead group. With 40km to go, the gap was just 1:20. This buffer dropped further as the kilometres progressed, while Jousseaume attacked from the lead group and by 20km to go it was two riders at the front, with Retegi joining the TotalEnergies rider. Despite the attempt to avoid the catch, at 6.5km to go the pair were reeled in.

That, however, opened up the opportunity for others to try and go, with the first wave of attacks neutralised by Aaron Gate (XDS-Astana) and while that opened up the way for another, the team of Malucelli was prepared to burn through some riders to keep it under control, but Riley Pickrell's Modern Adventure squad were also prepared to chip in. It turned out to be well worth their while.

*Cyclingnews attended Le Tour de Langkawi on an invitation/media package from the race that included travel and accommodation. In line with our editorial standards, our coverage is independent and was not subject to review, approval or influence by the organiser or any sponsor; no favourable coverage was promised or given in return.

Visma-Lease a Bike bring on Giorgia Bronzini as sports director
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
Bronzini, 43, is a two-time world champion. She retired in 2018 and spent three years as a director with Trek-Segafredo before joining Liv Racing for two seasons. For the past three years, she's worked with the Human Powered Health team. Her move to Visma-Lease a Bike brings her on the same team as her former sprint rival, Marianne Vos.

"Marianne and I raced against each other for many years, and there was always a lot of respect between us," Bronzini said in the team press release. "It is very special to now be on the same side and to have the opportunity to support Marianne achieve her goals. I'm really looking forward to that, as well as to working with the whole team and seeing what we can achieve together.

"I am happy and satisfied when the riders and staff are motivated and can say that we gave everything to reach our goal, and when everyone feels they contributed to what we achieved. You never do it alone. It is the team effort that allows you to win.""

Rutger Tijssen, the Visma-Lease a Bike women's team manager, said, "Giorgia knows women's cycling from the inside and had a strong understanding of the dynamics within the peloton. "That experience is very valuable to us.

"Giorgia's experience in the sport is obviously very valuable, but what also stood out to me was her enthusiasm and drive, and her willingness to work hard for her riders. We also found that we share a similar approach to guiding and supporting a team. That really appealed to me and was one of the reasons I wanted her to join our team."

"Giorgia will be dedicated to working with our younger riders, particularly on their tactical development and understanding of how to read a race," Tijssen said. "She also wants to help us to take the combination of performance and racing a step further. That way of thinking is something we value highly within our team, and especially with younger riders, there is still a lot to gain by bringing the two even more together."

items.title: The Real Reason Every Cycling Site Publishes Reviews at the Exact Same Time
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: It looks like a massive media conspiracy when a new bike drops. Here is what is actually happening behind the scenes on launch day.
items.lbText:
Welcome to Dropped , a new weekly road and gravel cycling newsletter from Velo that brings you the latest ideas we’re debating endlessly on group rides, and a look behind the scenes of our coverage.

I recently saw a comment—I read all of them, by the way—asking why every cycling outlet posted about the latest Canyon Grail at the exact same time. It’s a common question, often followed by claims that we’re being paid. It brings up a fair point: why is there coordination when a new bike launches, and how does it work? There’s nothing nefarious, nobody is getting paid, and there’s a good reason for it. Let’s look at the Canyon Grail launch .

A month out, Canyon asked if I wanted to review the bike, providing only a launch date and time. I checked my schedule, decided the bike could be interesting, said yes, and sent over my size. Then things went quiet, and the bike didn’t arrive before the launch. It’s not entirely unusual for that to happen, but that’s why I didn’t have a launch-day review for you.

Instead, two days before the launch, I got a press release with specs and photos. That’s all I had, but it was well done with thorough information. I’ve also been doing this for a long time, and I bring plenty of banked up knowledge and experience. I read through the details, figured out how the bike fit into the broader market, and pulled out the nuances I suspected other outlets might miss but felt were important. I could have asked follow-up questions if needed, but the info I needed was there. I wrote the story and scheduled it for the embargo time.

You’ll notice everything revolves around that launch date and time. It’s called an embargo, and it’s the real answer to why everything looks so coordinated. An embargo simply means a media outlet agrees to hold its coverage until a specific time in exchange for receiving advanced information about a product. It might look a bit like a conspiracy, especially when every brand agrees to the same embargo, but it actually creates much better coverage for readers.

It allows bike brands to share information freely ahead of time so we get a chance to ask questions and genuinely understand a product. If I am able to get the bike ahead of launch, I get to ride it, take photos and video, and follow up on technical details. If there are no shipping or production hiccups, I have a fully tested, accurate review ready to go exactly when the embargo lifts.

Ultimately, embargoes prevent a race to the bottom. If they didn’t exist, the second I heard about a new product, I’d have to slam something onto the internet as fast as possible just to get people’s attention first. I wouldn’t have time to test anything or ask a single question. With an embargo in place, I can focus on the bike and make sure the story or review is actually worth your time.

Does knowing how this works behind the scenes change how you view launch day coverage? Hit reply and let me know if the coordination ever felt like a conspiracy to you.

All things being equal, the Canyon launch went pretty well. It wasn’t perfect, since I didn’t have the bike in time to publish a review for the launch, but I had the information I needed ahead of launch time. I’ll call that the middle ground.

A really great launch happens when there’s plenty of lead time. For the Pinarello X-Series launch earlier this year, I had exactly that. I traveled to Italy to see the headquarters and talk with Fausto Pinarello to get a sense of the company. I spent time riding the bike and had the people who designed it available for questions. If something didn’t make sense, the person who made the decision was right there with an answer.

Of course, I always have to remember that those people are inherently trying to sell a bike. They absolutely paint a rosy picture, and I have to lean on my knowledge to judge what reality is and what consumers will actually want to know. I always try to do this with an eye toward the ideal consumer: who does the company think this bike is for, and is it truly right for that person? When I’m at the headquarters with the designers, I have the resources to find that out and make that judgment.

When I left Italy, I had all the photo and video assets I needed, and was able to grab as much time as I needed with the bike. To me, that is the ideal scenario. Sometimes, I’ll get a bike sent to me and rely on video meetings with designers and lots of emails to understand it. That works too, and it can be nice not to travel.

On the other end of the spectrum, sometimes there is zero lead time. I haven’t heard from a brand, and I suddenly get an email exactly at the embargo time with a press release. I have to scramble to get an article up and hope the press release contains the details I need. Half the time it doesn’t and I find myself zooming in on website photos trying to spot things like a third bottle cage mount and waiting on the brand to answer questions. When that happens, the coverage is not as thorough.

I’ve already worked this into the article a bit so far, but what you have to understand is that everyone has the same information. What I try to do is look for the story inside of that information. Why does this matter to the reader?

I look for the unique selling proposition, then I tell that story. I typically like to share what the company storyline is—although not always unchallenged—and then react to that story. Sometimes I think a brand missed the best story of the product, sometimes I think the story makes sense and the people involved nailed it, and occasionally I think a product just does not work.…

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘I’ll let the front office and my agency handle that’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Would you believe the Knicks play basketball next week!?

That’s right, and they do so against the Philadelphia 76ers of all teams, one that surely pays homage to the age of their roster with their moniker.

Here’s the latest we heard straight out of Tarrytown and elsewhere on Wednesday.

On eventually discussing Miles McBride’s contract situation with him:

“There will probably be a time and place where I talk to him about that because he’s human, and we all want what’s best for ourselves, our families, as well as the organization. That’s a nice balancing act, but at the end of the day, he wants to be here, we want him to be here, and that’s something that I have faith in Leon and Deuce’s representatives to figure that out.”

On staying out of the Knicks’ contract negotiations:

“It literally is the [salary] cap’s above my head. I don’t know how that works, and we’ve got a lot of moving parts as we all know. So I’m gonna let that unfold how it unfolds and in the meantime, we’re all just worried about how we can help each other on the court more than anything else because we know off the court, things get taken care of the right way here.”

On Gregg Popovich reaching out during the Knicks’ playoff run:

“[Pop] is grizzled, experienced. He understands how this works. We actually talked a couple of times during the playoffs. After OG’s tip-in, he called me and talked me through a lot of things. It was great to have conversations with him from time to time.”

On the support he received from the NBA coaching community after winning the championship:

“The coaching community is tight. Everybody wants everybody to do well because they know that the guy across from them is the one that really knows what I’m going through or the other guy’s going through. So because it’s that hard we really try to uplift one another whenever we can and when we won it, a lot of guys reached out if not everybody, and said congratulations in some way shape or form. It was great.”

On the Knicks looking for more centers:

“We’re looking for bigs. We’re looking at that [center] position heavily.”

On adding Tony Bradley and the need for center depth:

“Tony’s a veteran guy that’s still in his prime and has a good feel for the game, knows how to play the game the right way and he’s hurt us in the past. And, to be honest, when a guy hurts you in the past, you tend to remember him more than others. So to be able to add him to camp was a positive for us because, again, I said this last year: KAT has one of the most [difficult] spots out of everybody because I want to move him around when I play him at center. I want to play him at power forward, and at power forward, one through four is interchangeable.

“Same with OG [Anunoby]. OG we put him at the 5 last year. We probably will do it a little bit more this year as well. But to be able to do that, you’ve gotta have enough centers around on the team, so having Tony here with his skill set and feel is definitely a blessing because we’re looking at that position heavily.”

On planning to use Karl-Anthony Towns and OG at multiple positions:

“I want to play him at center, I want to play him at power forward.

“OG, we threw him at the five some last year. We probably will do a little bit more this year as well.”

On Josh Hart suddenly embracing the power forward label for the conditioning test:

“Josh was a power forward but when it came to the conditioning test, the power forwards and centers have an easier time [requirement]. Not much, but an easier time than guards. So all year I was calling him a power forward and he was cool with it but I could tell he didn’t really like it. But as soon as he heard about the conditioning test, he said he was a power forward.”

On wanting to remain with the Knicks for the rest of his career:

“Obviously, I love being in New York. I’d love to continue my career here, end my career here. Best fans, feel like we’ve done, obviously, something great this past year, and the years leading up to that. And I want to continue with this team.

“I’ve addressed a little bit earlier with some comments. But I’ll let the front office and my agency handle that.”

On being disappointed by the lack of a contract extension while remaining professional:

“It’s a little hard at times, but I’m gonna be a professional. I want to go out and do my job. So that’s in my ability, and to help the team win for as long as I’m with the team.”

On not allowing his contract uncertainty to affect his play:

“In a sense, every year you have to prove yourself. I feel like there’s uncertainty across the board for everybody in the league. Everybody’s going for big contracts and this and that. So I don’t let it really bother me. At the end of the day, I just want to go out there and give it my shot, play my best basketball.”

On whether he sees similarities in Mitchell Robinson’s departure and his situation:

“No, no. I mean, at the end of the day, it’s a business.”

On being fully healthy after recovering over the summer:

“I’m feeling a lot better. It’s kind of crazy thinking about how unhealthy I was playing through that playoff run. You go through surgery in an area where you need it. The easy medical term is sports hernia but it was a lot more complex than that. So having a summer under me, getting back fully healthy, it’s been so much better being able to move around how I want to move.

“They took my hip flexor, my abdomen and my groin and they pulled it and they put it in my pelvis and they did it on both sides. So trying to open a door, reach for a remote and everything you do is in that core, in that core section.

“So trying to keep up with those young guys in the Finals was tough.”

On the Knicks moving on from their championship summer:

“The summer that you’re champions, obviously, you only get to experience that for the summer, and then you’re right back to playing. I feel like we all had a good time. Everybody did the right thing over the summer. And we got right back to work when it was time to get back to work.”

On the Knicks’ championship bringing estranged families back together:

“I have people coming to me and saying, ‘I haven’t talked to my family member in 10 years,’ and I’m like, ‘Well, we should not be the reason that’s happening.’ But, you know, that’s cool to hear. Like I said, it’s not what I want to hear, necessarily, but those are cool moments to hear that what we’re doing on the court was able to bring people back together.”

On getting to take the Larry O’Brien Trophy to his high school:

“So you actually get to request it. You have to get approval from the front office and somebody in the front office is supposed to have it that weekend. They kindly let me have it, so shout out to Leon [Rose] for that. He let me have it for that weekend.”

On the security of his new Knicks contract:

“It definitely gives you a sense of perspective and appreciation that I’m grateful for. To be believed in and have that offered to me, for me and [his fiancée] Cammi to be able to stay here in New York and continue to grow this thing, it’s pretty special. To be asked to be a part of it is humbling and I’m grateful for it every day. It means a lot.”

On feeling proud after earning long-term security with the Knicks:

“In a way, it just makes me proud of myself. That’s why you work through the difficult times and the challenging and the questioning ones. Typically, there’s really good stuff on the other end of that. It feels good, it feels good to be a part of this moving forward. I don’t want to drop my level or get complacent or any of that, that’s definitely not the feeling. It’s more, it just feels good to know that you don’t have that heavy wave right on your ass again this training camp.”

On whether he has rewatched his Eastern Conference Finals 11-of-12-from-three performance:

“I haven’t watched it all back in full, no. I’ve seen little clips.”

On staying ready for his playoff opportunity:

“Playoffs are funny in that way, and I feel like I’ve been privy to that with my past experiences, where you sit and you’re not in the rotation, but you’re one or two games away from being called on, being relied on to do something. I don’t know, I kind of just had a feeling, I’ve seen this movie before. It worked out.”

On what his new contract means after years of uncertainty:

“Last couple of years I’ve been pretty open with you guys. It definitely gives you a sense of perspective and appreciation that I’m grateful for. To be believed in and have that offered to me, for me and Cammi to be able to stay here in New York and continue to grow this thing, it’s pretty special. To be asked to be a part of it is humbling and I’m grateful for it every day. It means a lot.”

On bringing the Larry O’Brien Trophy to his wedding:

“I took it on a date. I took it to my wedding. I asked to have it. I couldn’t have a wedding without Larry there, you know?”

On traveling with the trophy and still being amazed by winning it:

“He had a rider and all, and we made sure we got him there first class, and we got it done. So, I spent some time with the trophy this summer, and every time I see the trophy, I still can’t believe it.”

On being happy for his former Knicks teammates after their championship:

“I’m happy [for the Knicks], man. I kept in touch with guys. I’ve had a lot of great moments here in the city. I spent five years here, my family has grown here; so I was extremely excited, happy for those guys. A lot went into that; it’s not just myself, years before me.

“So, just happy for those guys. I was just last month on a trip with OG [Anunoby] in Brazil, just kicking it, talking with each other. So it was a great thing, not just for them, for the organization, [but] for the city that has craved that — we know how New York is — so has craved that winning formula, winning environment. And we plan to do the same thing here.”

On what Knicks and Yankees championships in the same year would mean:

“A Knicks championship in June and a Yankees World Series in October would bring world peace.”

On the Knicks’ championship run and his faith in the Yankees:

“It’s tough to go up against world champs like the Knicks, and the run they went on, it was so incredible with the ups and downs. But I got a lot of faith in these guys, man. We’ve got a special group here with a lot of grit.”

On the Yankees drawing inspiration from the Knicks:

“We’re definitely inspired by the Knicks, and we’ve got to keep the winning going in New York.”

On wanting the Yankees to create the same excitement in New York as the Knicks:

“Oh yeah, for sure, I can’t wait. I can’t wait until we go on that run. That’s what I want. I want the city to be on fire.

“It was amazing for me, especially for having friends on the (Knicks) team and being around them while it was going on. It was sick to watch.”

items.title: Taylor Phinney takes big step in comeback as he makes USA Cycling squad for UCI Track World Championships
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
The endurance and sprint squads were announced on Thursday, October 1, and having come out of retirement in April, Phinney will make up part of the team pursuit squad alongside new U23 road race World Champion Ashlin Barry, Graeme Frislie, Grand Koontz, and Anders Johnson.

Points Race silver medallist from 2025, Peter Moore, and Brendan Rhim make up the rest of the US men's endurance team, with no men's representation in the sprint events. Track Worlds will run from Wednesday, October 14, to Sunday, October 18.

In Santiago, Chile, last season, the US men's team finished fourth behind Denmark, Australia, and New Zealand, their best finish in the event since 1995, when they last won a medal.

It will be Phinney's first return to international track competition, having made his return to racing at the US Track National Championships back in August. There, he won gold in the team pursuit alongside Johnson, who he will be headed to China with, Colby Lange, and David Domonosky, at what was his first appearance at the event since 2008, aged 18.

A two-time World Champion in the track previously, Phinney won Individual Pursuit gold in Pruszków in 2009 and Ballerup in 2010. He also raced at the Beijing Olympics in 2008 on the track, finishing seventh as a teenager.

The US team will also be sending a strong presence to China for the women's endurance and sprint events, with former Olympic road race champion and reigning Olympic team pursuit gold medallist Kristen Faulkner as the standout name announced for Shanghai.

Fresh off the back of finishing 19th at the road Worlds in Montreal, Faulkner will be joined by talented 18-year-old Emma Jimenez Palos, Bethany Ingram, Megan Jastrab, Stephanie Lawrence and Anna Hicks for the endurance events.

After landing the USA's best-ever result of seventh in the women's team sprint in Chile last season, the trio of Kayla Hankins, Emily Hayes, and Hayley Yoslov will return to action together in China. Taking on the team event and individual sprints, they will also be joined by McKenna McKee.

items.title: Enve officially releases Tadej Pogačar's monument-winning wheelset
items.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
items.content:
Enve has launched a brand-new aero road wheel today: the SES 6.7 Pro.

This latest addition to the SES Pro range will be Enve's deepest and most aerodynamic road wheelset.

The 6.7 Pros have actually been hiding in plain sight for much of this year, as an unreleased wheelset from the American manufacturer.

Tadej Pogačar, as well as some of his teammates, have been racing and winning on the wheels for most of this year. Their win list is considerable, with Pogačar winning Milan-San Remo and Strade Bianche on them already.

Enve launched the SES 4.5 Pro wheelset just before the Tour de France last year, calling it 'The wheel Tadej asked for'.

The SES 6.7 Pro wheels will set you back £4,000 / $3750 / €4,600 if you are interested in emulating Pogačar and co's exploits.

Enve says this new wheelset is 'designed to deliver even greater speed while maintaining stability and confidence'.

The previous Enve SES 6.7 wheelset used a 60mm / 66mm rim depth combination, which, as of January 1st 2026, fell foul of the UCI maximum rim depth ruling of 65mm.

This major overhaul employs a 59mm front rim and a 65mm deep rear rim to stay UCI-compliant. Front and rear rims are 30.5mm's wide externally, and have front- and rear-specific rim shapes.

The wheels are optimised around 28mm tyres and have been developed by aerodynamicist and Drag 2 Zero founder Simon Smart, who has worked with Enve since 2009.

In terms of specs, the wheelset weighs in at 1495 grams with tubeless valves and tapes, and the brand says it is for tubeless-compatible tyres only.

The rims have a 22.5mm wide internal rim width with a hooked rim. Enve says they are for flat and rolling terrain.

Both wheels have a spoke count of 24 and use silver Alpina spokes and alloy spoke nipples.

The wheels are built around silver Enve Innerdrive Pro hubs, which use a lighter 40-tooth engagement ratchet and custom ratchet spring. The Enve Pro Ceramic bearings have non-contact inboard seals and low-contact outboard seals for slightly more protection.

Enve says the wheels were developed using CFD, wind tunnel testing and validation on the road.

They have been tested in a wind tunnel in a bike at 'elite and amateur speeds alike'.

Whilst Enve hasn't gone as far as to provide a white paper or in-depth testing numbers for the wheelset (possibly due to a certain top WorldTour team using them), they have provided some testing info and a comparison against a sizeable range of competitor wheelsets, which we don't always see.

The brand has tested against various competitors, including Vision, Roval, Hunt and Princeton.

Check out the graphs below for yourself, but the SES 6.7 Pro wheels were top aero performers, not counting the faster Enve disc wheel / 100mm front wheel combo, which isn't used in road races.

items.title: Swiss climber Steffi Häberlin switches SD Worx for Canyon-SRAM with 'more to unlock' – Analysis
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Canyon-SRAM announced the signing of Swiss rider Steffi Häberlin, who joins the German team after spending two years at SD Worx-Protime.

Häberlin is a fairly recent convert to road cycling, having started racing mountain bikes in 2020. She quickly found success, winning the Swiss MTB marathon title the same year and taking European silver in the same event a year later.

She turned pro on the road just last year, joining SD Worx and winning the Swiss road title as well as finishing fifth at the Tour de Romandie Fémninin. This season, she's progressed further, defending her national title, winning the recent Tour de Gatineau, and scoring top-10 finishes at the UAE Tour and Tour de Suisse.

28-year-old Häberlin is hoping to continue her rapid progression with her new team.

"Canyon-SRAM is an ambitious team, but at the same time I don’t think that the human side of the sport gets lost," she said.

"I've had the feeling that Canyon-SRAM really tries to support each rider individually, and get the most out of everyone. I also find it commendable that Canyon-SRAM takes responsibility for the next generation through the Generation team."

Häberlin joins fellow Swiss racer Jasmin Liechti on the incoming list for Canyon, while Dutch multi-disciplinarian Shirin van Anrooij also joins next month ahead of the cyclocross season.

Häberlin will embark on her third season in the Women's WorldTour next season, and she said any doubts about her place at the top level of road cycling are "long gone."

"My first contract was a big change for me because I had only been cycling for four years, and that was mainly as a cross-country mountain biker. I had been thinking about making the switch to the road for quite some time, but I didn't really know what to expect or whether it was the right decision for me at that time," she said.

"Those doubts are long gone now, and I'm really happy to be a road cyclist. I see this next step as a great opportunity to keep learning and developing as a rider, and to gather more race days."

For SD Worx-Protime, Häberlin's departure is the sixth for 2027, joining Marta Lach (Human Powered Health), Julia Kopecký, Blanka Vas (both Lidl-Trek), Femke Markus (Visma-Lease a Bike), and Elena Cecchini (retiring).

To date, the Dutch team have brought in four riders in the shape of Cédrine Kerbaol, Axelle Dubau-Prévot (EF Education-Oatly), Rachele Barbieri (Picnic-PostNL), and Eline Jansen (VolkerWessels).

items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
You don’t know how much I missed #KnicksSZN. Actually, if you’re reading this… I mean, you probably know as well.

Here’s the latest from Tarrytown and other NBA-related places.

  • Karl-Anthony Towns opened up extensively about what finally becoming an NBA champion meant after years of criticism. In an interview with The Athletic, he also detailed how during the Knicks’ miserable 2-9 January stretch and amid Giannis Antetokounmpo trade rumors, he and Jordyn Woods were apparently checking Milwaukee real estate.

“We were on Zillow looking at Milwaukee. Like, ‘Hey, babe, I went around town, and it’s not that bad. This could be a good spot right here.’”

  • Towns’ extension remains a significant unresolved issue, and ESPN’s Malika Andrews reported KAT is willing to take a discount similar in spirit to Brunson’s sacrifice… but “the pay cut that the Knicks are asking him to take, he views as unreasonable.” Uh, oh.
  • Isiah Thomas is returning to the organization, folks. He’ll be part of the NYK board of directors. The move is part of the recently confirmed MSG split of the Rangers and the Knicks.
  • The Knicks still haven’t decided whether they will make the traditional championship visit to the White House despite James Dolan saying in June that the organization had accepted an invitation.
  • Bobby Marks’ Knicks training-camp snapshot for ESPN underscores how tight the roster math is, with the pundit watching “the frontcourt and final roster spots” as the key remaining thing to solve before New York kicks off its title-defense season.
  • Former Knicks guard J.R. Smith was arrested in Texas on a charge of assault causing bodily injury-family violence after police said a traffic stop revealed an active warrant from the Southlake Police Department.
  • Phoenix Suns villain Dillon Brooks has been charged with driving under the influence, per TMZ. Being arrested is a trend these days.
  • About LeBron’s Philadelphia era, James is indeed splitting his time between New York City and Philadelphia and commuting by helicopter.
  • The NBA is reportedly gaining momentum toward agreements with major European soccer clubs for its planned NBA Europe competition, which is targeted to launch next fall.
  • OAKAAK Carmelo Anthony knows very clearly what he’d do with Jalen Duren if he were in charge of the Pistons’ operations.
  • Shortly after the Grizzlies released D’Angelo Russell, the mighty point guard and former No. 2 overall pick from the 2015 NBA draft is flying to China to play for the Shanghai Sharks, and joining an illustrious list of NBA alumni to play for the organization.
  • Tyler Herro was traded from the Heat to the Bucks, but he’s happy to leave the “Capital of Distraction” for… a place somewhere in Wisconsin?
  • Former Knicks’ first-round pick Kristaps Porzingis won’t be able to participate in the Warriors’ training camp due to an undisclosed “health issue.” Somebody give this man a break.
  • Nikola Jokic isn’t close to turning his full attention to horses.
  • The New York Liberty just became the first-ever No. 8 seed to send the No. 1 seed (Minnesota Lynx) home in the WNBA playoffs. Now, let’s finish this business.

items.title: Ion Izagirre's dream farewell in Il Lombardia wrecked by broken wrist in training accident
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
Ion Izagirre's hopes of a dream sendoff to a highly successful pro career at Il Lombardia have been dashed this week after crashing during a training ride and breaking his wrist.

One of the sport's best-known and most versatile racers, the 37-year-old Basque had announced his retirement earlier this season, in which he has won two well-known Classics, the Memorial Miguel Indurain – for a third time – and the Memorial Marco Pantani, the 20th victory of his career.

This season he also took fourth in his home race of La Itzulia, which he won back in 2019, as well as seventh in Paris-Nice and La Fleche Wallonne.

However, his idea of going out on a high note at Il Lombardia, a race where he finished fourth in 2024 and sixth in 2018, has been wrecked by his training accident, which left him with a broken left wrist.

Cofidis published the news about his crash on social media, wishing him a "speedy and fast recovery," and recognising it was the end of his season.

Izagirre's untimely exit from the road racing side of the sport should not detract from a hugely prestigious career in which the wins never ceased, even in his final season. These included stage victories in all three Grand Tours, Paris-Nice, and the Tour de Romandie, as well as overall titles at the Tour de Pologne and Itzulia Basque Country.

Izagirre turned pro back in 2010 with the small Conti' team, Orbea-Oreka SDA, before continuing his career at WorldTour level with Euskaltel-Euskadi, Movistar, Bahrain-Merida, Astana and finally Cofidis.

items.title: 'I survived all of this' – Challengers fight back on queen stage of Tour de Langkawi but Lennart Jasch proves his GC fortitude
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
There have been plenty of tests for Lennart Jasch (Tudor Pro Cycling) this week at Le Tour de Langkawi; Thursday was perhaps the biggest. This was the queen stage, the day on the bike which will most likely have set him on the path towards riding all the way through to the end of the eighth stage with the orange leader's jersey on his back, in not just his first attempt at the race but also in his first season as a professional and his first time as a team leader.

Right from the beginning, as he fronted up to the pre-race media conference, he has looked anything but green, handling the responsibilities of being in the spotlight with a cheery but understated confidence and on the road, he has been measured, though anything but understated, as he has deftly tackled the task at hand.

Two more tough summit finishes remained, though, and challengers in the form of the Caja Rural-Seguros RGA duo of Abel Balderstone and Jan Castellon lay just 26 and 42 seconds behind. The big question was whether the 25-year-old former speed skater who only stepped up from the Tudor development squad in the middle of this season had not just the legs but the level-headedness which is often aided by experience to keep it.

The path of the next climbing test, stage 4, was a promising sign given the restraint shown to play the longer game as his Tudor team let a break who did not threaten his overall position run away with the win

"You also need to manage the power you have over the whole time, I mean doesn't help when we maybe take a third place or something today, but then we don't have anyone the last three stages? So yeah, you have to choose the battles you want to win. I would say," said Jasch after Wednesday's stage 4 in the Cameron Highlands.

And he already had his third stage win for the season after the performance on Gunung Jerai, so now the battle he wanted to chase was clearly his first overall victory.

Even though the two wins he had already swept up before starting the Tour de Langkawi left him feeling that there was no pressure, given what he had already achieved, it was hard not to feel at least some nerves heading into Thursday's all-important day of racing, the Genting Highlands queen stage.

Though once again Jasch delivered despite the chaos and challengers coming from every direction. A break of two were well up the road – the gap at five minutes at the start of the climb – and one of those was Josh Burnett (Burgos Burpellet BH), who was only 3:20 behind overall at the start of the day. Plus, of course, the riders in the group with Jasch were also going to try and test him every step of the way to see if they could find some weakness in his armour.

Right from the start there were waves of attempts to get into the break, a split in the peloton, a crash in front of Lennart and also the lengthy gap to the leading two, including the well-positioned Burnett.

"There are a lot of points where you can be nervous, but yeah, in the end, you always should be as calm as possible. And now I'm really, really happy that I'm sitting here still in the orange jersey, and I survived all of this," Jasch told the assembled media in the Genting Highlands after taking third on the stage and comfortably holding his GC lead.

In fact, he even extended his lead to 26 seconds on second-placed Balderstone, a commanding position to be in given that the remaining stages are largely flat.

"I think I can be quite confident, but yeah, in the end, it's still three more stages to come, and you never know what happens, so let's keep fighting," said Jasch.

And no matter what now happens in Malaysia, his performance so far in his first role as a leader chasing overall victory is bound to mean we will see him continuing the GC fight in future, because there can now be little doubt about his ability to deliver in that role.

*Cyclingnews attended Le Tour de Langkawi on an invitation/media package from the race that included travel and accommodation.
