items.title: From the Velodrome to Space: US Track Champion Christina Birch Named NASA Mission Pilot
items.author: ahood
items.content: After swapping skinsuits for spacesuits, ex-track cyclist and Team USA member Christina Birch prepares for her first spaceflight with NASA in 2027.
items.lbText:
Former track cyclist turned astronaut Christina Birch has been named to NASA’s SpaceX Crew-14 mission. (Photo: Space-X/Getty Images)

Most retired cyclists settle for a new challenge like taking on gravel or becoming a TV commentator.

The former U.S. national team track cyclist and 11-time national champion has been named pilot of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-14 mission to the International Space Station, with launch scheduled spring 2027.

Birch, 39, will make her first spaceflight alongside commander Kayla Barron, Japan’s Makoto Suwa, and Russian cosmonaut Arutyun Kiviryan, NASA officials confirmed.

Their assignment involves “scientific investigations and technology demonstrations to help prepare humans for future exploration missions to the moon and Mars.”

That is quite a career move for someone whose previous office job called for steep banking, fixed gears, and an aerodynamic tuck on the boards.

Before swapping skinsuits for spacesuits, Birch won three World Cup medals and two Pan American Games gold medals across the team pursuit and Madison with Team USA .

She also made the U.S. Olympic long team for the 2021 Tokyo Games for the team pursuit squad that later won the bronze medal.

And cycling was already something of a career change for this overachiever.

Birch earned degrees in mathematics and biochemistry and molecular biophysics at the University of Arizona, then a doctorate in biological engineering at MIT.

She taught bioengineering before leaving to pursue elite track racing. She started racing on the track to cross-train for her initial passion in cyclocross.

And that was all before NASA selected her as an astronaut candidate in 2021.

In an Instagram post reflecting on astronaut training, Birch made some connections between cycling and her upcoming space adventure.

In cycling, she explained the sport generally rewards doing everything faster, while spaceflight means preparing to succeed when things go horribly wrong.

Her early training included survival camp in the woods of Alabama, underwater sessions to simulate space walks, and learning to fly jets, and she still found time to race the Leadville Trail 100 MTB race and run a marathon.

“Our goal, then, is to cross the finish line together, no matter the method or speed,” she wrote. “So we practice … and practice … and practice our contingency plans until we are sure that, even on our average days, we succeed in our mission.”

She recently served as a capsule communicator to crews during the Artemis II mission in 2026 in the first space mission to the moon since the 1970s.

Her favorite movie? Interstellar , of course.

Birch’s bike handling skills just might come in handy in orbit.

items.title: Nicolas Breuillard wins stage 5 of Le Tour de Langkawi as Lennart Jasch keeps firm grip on overall lead in Genting Highlands queen stage
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
Nicolas Breuillard (TotalEnergies) bounced back from illness earlier in Le Tour de Langkawi to claim the final summit finish of the eight-stage race, winning in the Genting Highlands on stage 5 after dropping his break companion Josh Burnett (Burgos-Burpellet BH) in the final kilometres, and holding off a chase including GC leader Lennart Jasch (Tudor Pro Cycling).

On Thursday Jasch, also with the help of the third-place time bonus, extended his lead on Abel Balderstone (Caja Rural-Seguros RGA) to 26 seconds and put Jan Castellon (Caja Rural-Seguros RGA ) 42 seconds behind. It's going to now be hard to budge the first-year professional from that top spot given the flat terrain ahead.

"The race isn't over yet but we are a big big step closer to the finish line in terms of the GC I would say," said Jasch in a post stage interview.

For Breuillard and TotalEnergies, the team of last year's overall winner Joris Delbove, it was a welcome turn of fortunes for the rider and squad. They first had to give their team leader, Jordan Jegat, over as a late replacement for the French team at the Road World Championships, then they lost a retiring Geoffrey Bouchard to a stage 1 crash and then Breuillard had his problems too.

"I came here for the GC and I fell sick in the start of the day in Malaysia, after this I wanted to win a stage, and I'm very happy with that," said the French rider, who made his intentions clear on stage 5 when he went out into the break with a teammate Valentin Retailleau alongside, who helped pull out the margin between the peloton and the break to around five minutes at the start of the 22km climb.

The 125.7km stage from Tapah to the Genting Highlands started with 111 riders and among those missing was the key GC hope for Picnic PostNL, Mattia Gaffuri, who was caught up in a crash early on stage 4 but rode on and finished with the front group of contenders to retain his seventh spot overall. However, he'd done it with a broken hand.

"He was really motivated for these two days, but yeah, yesterday, showed a really good spirit to fight to the finish, so he did more than 120k with the hand broken and still held a group of 30 guys," Picnic PostNL sports director Melvin Rulliere told ahead of the stage.

That meant there was plenty of incentive for both Picnic PostNL and many other teams that hadn't had the race go their way so far to play an aggressive hand. This was the last chance for the climbers to make a real difference as the road wound its way up through the lush jungle and once again to the top of the climb, which rounded off an otherwise flat stage.

The fierce efforts to get in the break even caused a brief split in the peloton at one point, which Jasch was on the wrong side of.

Among an early escape there was Matthew Peace (Picnic PostNL), Nicolas Breuillard and Valentin Retailleau of (TotalEnergies) and Mervin Corpuz (7/Eleven Cliqq) but they were pulled back in at 13km to go and then a whole new round of attacking began.

Finally a group of six was established up front with Breuillard and Retailleau again part of the group, along with Fernando Gaviria (Caja Rural-Serguros RGA), Josh Burnett and Rodrigo Alvarez (Burgos Burpellet-BH) and Robin Carpenter (Modern Adventure).

Edward Cruz (Bardiani CSF 7 Saber) also ultimately made the junction, but not surprisingly sprinter Gaviria fell away as the climbing began. Retailleau, who was working for teammate Breuillard, also fell away after putting in a huge volume of work to set his teammate up with as big a gap as possible, which ended up being five minutes near the bottom of the climb.

Others fell away and ultimately it came down to Burnett and Breuillard out the front, with Burnett at times virtually threatening Jasch's lead. However in the final kilometres the Burgos-Burpellet rider from New Zealand fell away from his break companion. Though he didn't let the gap stretch far, holding off the pursuing group behind which Jasch lead over the line. The race leader crossed the line just ahead of Castellon and then a further two seconds back it was José Manuel Díaz (Burgos-Burpellet-BH) and Balderstone.
